records.originEnglish: The matter is as follows. Berakhot relates that he saw him rejoicing greatly and said to him: “It is written, ‘In all sadness there is gain.’” He answered: “I am wearing tefillin.” Tefillin indicate that he is bound to the beginning of thought, as it is said: “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first of His produce,” and so forth. This is when one merits to straighten the heart completely; the upright are destined for joy, as it is written: “Joy for the upright of heart.” Likewise, regarding Abraham’s feast, Tosafot in Shabbat cites Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer: “On the day of higamel” means on the day of heh-gimel, eight, he circumcised—the eighth day of circumcision. Isaac was the first to be circumcised at eight days. Since the infant is circumcised on the eighth day without his knowledge and thereby becomes an Israelite, this indicates that he is bound at the root, at the beginning of thought.

records.targetEnglish: Berakhot relates: He saw him rejoicing greatly and said, “It is written, ‘Rejoice with trembling.’” He answered, “I am wearing tefillin,” and so forth. What, seemingly, did he answer? It is forbidden to fill one’s mouth with laughter in this world, and it is written, “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter”—specifically then! But tefillin indicate that one is bound to the root of thought: “In the beginning”—for Israel, and so forth. Israel crowns the Holy One, blessed be He, with the splendor of tefillin, proclaiming “The Lord is one”; and the Holy One, blessed be He, praises Israel’s excellence, as stated there. This is “All the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you”—these are the tefillin of the head. Specifically “upon you”: the head tefillin are like a crown upon the head. The holy Zohar says that the word az, “then,” indicates when the light of Atika shines: the alef pierces the darkness, and so forth, and they reach the zayin—alef-zayin. This is “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter.” In the future the aspect called “He” will be revealed and shine; hence the expression “on that day,” when that aspect of “He,” indicating Atika, will shine like day. It is specifically “then” that our mouth will be filled with laughter. This is the answer “I am wearing tefillin”: when an Israelite puts on tefillin, a revelation of Atika’s light shines within him, because he is bound to the root. This too is “then,” as stated.
records.explanation: The Chanukah passage supplies the missing step between tefillin and joy: tefillin can make a measure of the light associated with the future “then” present now. Its reciprocal crowns—Israel proclaiming God’s unity and God praising Israel—explain why the sign concerns an existing bond, rather than the mere outward performance of a mitzvah. This deepens the same reply in Lech Lecha while retaining its condition of a heart made upright.

records.targetEnglish: “Honor”—these are tefillin. The principal bond Israel has with words of Torah is alluded to in tefillin. A passage of Torah is written and concealed in the clothing of the tefillin’s compartments, and the person who wears them is considered as though he fulfilled the whole Torah through the positive commandment, “You shall meditate upon it day and night.” As the Midrash says: Israel said, “Master of the universe, we wish to labor in Torah day and night,” and so forth. The Holy One, blessed be He, answered: “Fulfill the commandment of tefillin, and I account it to you as though you labored in Torah day and night.” A person must sometimes occupy himself with bodily needs. Tefillin indicate that, just as a passage of Torah is hidden deep within their clothing, words of Torah are found within the depths of all the garments into which Israel enters; no Israelite soul enters garments entirely devoid of Torah. Therefore Berakhot relates that he saw him rejoicing greatly, and he answered, “I am wearing tefillin.” That is: since I put on tefillin, you can infer that I recognize well the words of Torah hidden in all the expansiveness you see in me. Tefillin allude to such a great bond that no garment of Israel is devoid of a connection to His light. This is “Honor”—these are tefillin.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim interprets the same reply through the structure of tefillin: Torah remains within a covering. It therefore explains the relation between outward expansiveness and an inward bond that is not immediately visible. The speaker’s explicit recognition of the Torah within his joy is essential; the passage does not make outward exuberance alone proof of the straightened heart described in Lech Lecha.

records.targetEnglish: Therefore they expounded Abraham our father’s “great feast” as the meal the Holy One, blessed be He, will make for the righteous on the day He bestows His kindness upon Isaac’s descendants, as stated in Pesachim. The essence of the future meal is the revelation of the secrets of Torah and the light of God, as the Rambam writes in the eighth chapter of the Laws of Repentance. Although the Raavad objects to him, we have already said that the Rambam’s view is explicit in the Midrash HaNeelam; examine it there. This is the future “great feast”: the wine of the Oral Torah, when it will be explicit that it comes from the blessed God. This cannot be revealed for as long as a person remains in the body. It is called a “great feast” because it will be explicit that the Great One of the worlds is there: the Holy One, blessed be He, will reveal the secrets to the righteous.
records.explanation: The Purim discourse identifies what the future feast reveals: the divine source of Torah’s secrets, including Oral Torah that can appear to originate solely in human discovery. That gives content to Lech Lecha’s “light of the Infinite.” Its final qualification also matters: the complete revelation lies beyond embodied life, so the present circumcision meal is described as a participation or foretaste, not as that future revelation in its entirety.

records.targetEnglish: This is what they said: in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a great meal for Isaac’s descendants. He associated the greatness with Isaac because Israel will merit this recompense through his quality. Since Israel endured many restrictions in this world for the honor of Heaven and did not give their will free expansion at all because of their fear of the blessed God, the corresponding measure is that the Holy One, blessed be He, will make them a great meal. That is, He will show them that the whole earth is full of His glory. Isaac our father will stand at the head of the governance, as stated in the writings of the Ari; and as stated in the holy Zohar: “I will say to the north, Give”—in you I placed all the good things and all the treasures of the world.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why this same future feast is attached specifically to Isaac’s descendants. Restricted self-expansion for the sake of Heaven is answered by the discovery that God’s glory fills the whole earth. This supplies a relation between restraint and the feast’s unbounded goodness, illuminating why Lech Lecha links the meal of circumcision to a future joy of the upright heart.

records.originEnglish: The matter of intoxication resembles what we find in Megillah: “A person is obliged to become intoxicated on Purim,” and so forth. Elsewhere in holiness we find only drinking wine, as Rav Nachman said: “Until I have drunk a quarter-log of wine, my mind is not clear”—not intoxication, which confuses the mind. But when Amalek, the beginning of the impure side, is erased, Israel is clarified as being bound to the beginning of thought. Thus they expounded “The Jews had light, joy, gladness, and honor”: “Honor”—these are tefillin. The tefillin of the head indicate that Israel is bound to the beginning of thought. When this becomes clear, intoxication too can be in holiness. The tribes likewise felt this holiness then, at the Shabbat meal Joseph made for them.
records.themeTitle: Purim reveals a bond deeper than conscious effort
records.themeSummary: The paragraph distinguishes wine that clears the mind from Purim’s intoxication. Its explanation rests on the disclosure of Israel’s prior bond after Amalek’s opposition is removed, and then applies that distinction to Joseph’s Shabbat meal.
records.targetHebrew: וְ״אֶסְתֵּר — סוֹף כָּל הַנִּסִּים״ (יוֹמָא כ״ט עַמּוּד א׳), הוּא סוֹף כָּל קְדֻשַּׁת הַזְּמַנִּים עַד שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לִקְדֻשַּׁת יוֹם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שְׁבִיתָה מִמְּלָאכָה, דְּיוֹם טוֹב לֹא קִבְּלוּ, רַק ״מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָה״ (מְגִלָּה ה׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) וְהוּא נָעוּץ בִּתְחִלָּתָן שֶׁל קְדֻשַּׁת הַזְּמַנִּים, שֶׁהוּא קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא רֹאשׁ כָּל הַנִּסִּים בִּבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן, וְהַכֹּל בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא נַעֲשָׂה בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּידְהוּ וְשֶׁהֵם מְקַדְּשֵׁי, דְּעַדַיִין לֹא הָיוּ בָּעוֹלָם וְהַסּוֹף, שֶׁהוּא יְמֵי הַפּוּרִים, בּוֹ נִתְגַּלָּה דְּגַם כָּל הַקְּדוּשָׁה דְּ״יִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי לִזְמַנֵּי״ (בְּרָכוֹת מ״ט עַמּוּד א׳) אֵינוֹ מִצַּד עַצְמָם וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם רַק הַכֹּל בִּקְדוּשָׁה דִּקְבוּעָא וְקַיָּימָא בְּקִרְבָּם וְזֶה מִתְבָּרֵר בִּשְׁעַת הַבִּיסּוּם ״עַד דְּלֹא יָדַע״ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל (מְגִלָּה ז׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) דְּמִתְגַּלֶּה דְּעַצְמִיּוּתָם — כּוּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳:
records.targetEnglish: “Esther—the end of all the miracles” is the culmination of the holiness of the appointed times, reaching the holiness of a day without cessation from labor. They did not accept it as a festival [prohibiting labor], but only as “feasting and joy.” Its end is bound to the beginning of the holiness of the appointed times: the holiness of Shabbat, the beginning of all miracles in the creation of the entire world from nothing. All this was for Israel, although it did not arise through their awakening or their sanctification, since they were not yet in the world. At the end, the days of Purim, it was revealed that even all the holiness of “Israel sanctifies the appointed times” does not come from themselves and their effort, but entirely from the holiness fixed and enduring within them. This is clarified at the time of intoxication “until he does not know,” as explained above: their very essence is revealed as entirely holy to the Lord.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim makes explicit the relation between Shabbat and Purim that Lech Lecha invokes. Shabbat expresses a holiness preceding Israel’s effort; Purim reveals that prior holiness even within times Israel actively sanctifies. Thus the loss of ordinary knowledge functions in the argument as disclosure of a bond that was never produced by that knowledge. This is an explanation of the author’s Purim distinction, not a general license to seek holiness through intoxication.

records.originHebrew: וְעִנְיַן הַשִּׁכְרוּת הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ (מְגִילָּה ז עַמּוּד ב): "מִיחַיַּיב אִינִישׁ לִבְסוֹמֵי בְּפוּרַיָּא וְכוּלֵי", אַף שֶׁלֹּא מָצִינוּ בִּקְדוּשָׁה רַק לִשְׁתּוֹת יַיִן, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מָצִינוּ בְּרַב נַחְמָן שֶׁאָמַר: "כָּל כַּמָּה דְּלָא שָׁתֵינָא רְבִיעֲתָא דְּחַמְרָא לָא צִילָאי דַּעְתַּאי", אֲבָל לֹא "לִבְסוֹמֵי" שֶׁמְּבַלְבֵּל הַדַּעַת! אַךְ בִּמְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק שֶׁהוּא רֵאשִׁית דִּקְלִיפָּה, וְאָז מִתְבָּרְרִין יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁקְּשׁוּרִים בְּרֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה; וְכֵן נִדְרָשׁ: "'לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה וְשִׂמְחָה וְשָׂשׂוֹן וִיקָר' – 'וִיקָר', אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין וְכוּלֵי", וּתְפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ מוֹרֶה שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל קְשׁוּרִים בְּרֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה. וּכְשֶׁמִּתְבָּרֵר זֶה, אָז יֵשׁ גַּם שִׁכְרוּת בִּקְדוּשָׁה; וְכֵן הִרְגִּישׁוּ אָז הַשְּׁבָטִים הַקְּדוּשָׁה בִּסְעוּדַת שַׁבָּת שֶׁעָשָׂה יוֹסֵף לָהֶם.
records.originEnglish: The matter of intoxication resembles what we find in Megillah: “A person is obliged to become intoxicated on Purim,” and so forth. Elsewhere in holiness we find only drinking wine, as Rav Nachman said: “Until I have drunk a quarter-log of wine, my mind is not clear”—not intoxication, which confuses the mind. But when Amalek, the beginning of the impure side, is erased, Israel is clarified as being bound to the beginning of thought. Thus they expounded “The Jews had light, joy, gladness, and honor”: “Honor”—these are tefillin. The tefillin of the head indicate that Israel is bound to the beginning of thought. When this becomes clear, intoxication too can be in holiness. The tribes likewise felt this holiness then, at the Shabbat meal Joseph made for them.

records.targetHebrew: הנה בזה היום האיר השי"ת בהתגלות מפורש לישראל האור מכל אלו הדברים שעמלק מכחיש אותם לזה נאמר ליהודים היתה אורה וכמבואר בגמ' שם אורה זו תורה וכן הוא אומר כי נר מצוה ותורה אור כי ענין תורה הוא כמבואר בזוה"ק (מצורע נג:) מאי תורה דאורי וגלי במה דהוה סתים דלא אתידע וכו' היינו כי כל בריאת עולם הוא שהלביש השי"ת את האור והסתיר אותו בכל הלבושים של עוה"ז. וע"י ד"ת יכולין לבוא למקור האור שהוא סתים בכל הלבושים. ועמלק מכחיש זאת ואמר מאחר שהשי"ת העלים והסתיר את האור בלבושים אי אפשר בעוה"ז לגלות את האור כי אם הי' רצונו ית' בהתגלות אור לא הסתירו בלבושי עוה"ז וכיון שברא השי"ת עוה"ז מוכח שרצונו ית' הוא בהסתרת האור
records.targetEnglish: On this day the blessed God openly illuminated for Israel the light of all those things that Amalek denies. Therefore it says, “The Jews had light,” as the Talmud explains: “Light”—this is Torah, as it is said, “For a commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light.” The meaning of Torah is as the holy Zohar explains: “What is Torah? That which teaches and reveals what had been concealed and unknown.” The entire creation of the world is that the blessed God clothed the light and concealed it within all the garments of this world. Through words of Torah one can come to the source of the light hidden within all those garments. Amalek denies this and says: since the blessed God hid and concealed the light in garments, it is impossible to reveal the light in this world. If His will had been to reveal light, He would not have concealed it in the garments of this world; since He created this world, it supposedly proves that His will is to conceal the light.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim identifies a particular denial represented by Amalek: concealment is treated as proof that the divine light cannot be reached within worldly life. Purim discloses the bond that this argument denies. This clarifies what must be removed for Lech Lecha’s “beginning of thought” to become manifest; Sod Yesharim’s account concerns the revelation of the bond through Torah and does not itself derive the practice of intoxication.

records.originHebrew: וְכֵן מַה דִּכְתִיב בְּיִצְחָק: "וַיָּבֵא לוֹ יַיִן וַיֵּשְׁתְּ", שָׁם כְּתִיב: "וָאֹכַל מִכֹּל", וְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יז עַמּוּד א): "שְׁלֹשָׁה הִטְעִימָן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְכוּלֵי, יִצְחָק דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ 'מִכֹּל'", וְאִיתָא (בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סז): "'וָאֹכַל מִכֹּל' – מִכָּל טוֹב שֶׁהוּא מְתוּקָּן לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא"; וְכֵיוָן שֶׁזָּכָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּיֵצֶר הָרָע – הוּתַּר לוֹ הַיַּיִן.
records.originEnglish: Likewise, where it is written of Isaac, “He brought him wine, and he drank,” it also says, “I ate of all.” The Talmud in Bava Batra says: “There were three whom the Holy One, blessed be He, gave a foretaste of the world to come in this world,” including Isaac, of whom it is written “of all.” Bereishit Rabbah says: “‘I ate of all’—of all the good prepared for the future.” Since he merited a foretaste of the world to come in this world, without the evil inclination, wine was permitted to him.
records.themeTitle: Isaac’s wine belongs to the joy of the future blessings
records.themeSummary: The permission attributed to Isaac depends on his actual tasting of life without the evil inclination. The verse’s “of all” supplies the condition, rather than the mere fact that wine was brought to him.
records.targetHebrew: וְאַף יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם זָכָה לִטְעוֹם מִיַּיִן זֶה בַּיַּיִן שֶׁהֵבִיא לוֹ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּשֶׁקִּבֵּל הַבְּרָכוֹת שֶׁעִיקָּרָן בְּרָכוֹת שֶׁלֶּעָתִיד לָבוֹא וְהִתְגַּבְּרוּתוֹ עַל עֵשָׂו שֶׁהוּא הַיַּיִן הַמֵּבִיא יְלָלָה מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יַיִן שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנָּתַן לְיִצְחָק הֵבִיא שִׂמְחָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁיְּבָרְכוֹ וְכָל הָאָבוֹת זָכוּ לְחַיִּים שֶׁלֹּא בְּצַעַר וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּיֵצֶר הָרָע כְּמָה שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ
records.targetEnglish: Isaac our father too merited to taste this wine through the wine Jacob our father brought him when he received the blessings. Their principal content is the blessings of the future and his prevailing over Esau, who is the wine that brings wailing. By contrast, Jacob’s wine, which he gave Isaac, brought joy into his heart so that he would bless him. All the patriarchs merited life without sorrow and without the evil inclination, as stated in Tanna de-Vei Eliyahu.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz relates Isaac’s wine to the actual work of the scene: blessing Jacob with the future good and overcoming the opposing force associated with Esau. It explains why this wine brings a different kind of joy. The full paragraph also insists that even Jacob’s rightful desire for settled life could precede its time, which supports Lech Lecha’s distinction between a promised attainment and one already reached.

records.originHebrew: וְהַטַּעַם, שֶׁאַף יַיִן זֶה הָיָה יַיִן דְּמִצְוָה, דְּאִיתָא בְּפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י בְּשֵׁם מִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה: שֶׁרָמַז לוֹ עַל הַמְּנָחוֹת וְעַל הַנְּסָכִים וְכוּלֵי, וְהַיְינוּ עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (יוֹמָא עא עַמּוּד א): "הָרוֹצֶה לְנַסֵּךְ יַיִן עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ – יְמַלֵּא גְּרוֹנָם שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים יַיִן", וְאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת י עַמּוּד ב): "כָּל הַמְאָרֵחַ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וְכוּלֵי מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ מַקְרִיב תְּמִידִין"; וְהוּא, כְּשֶׁמַּאֲכִיל לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם בָּשָׂר הוּא כְּמַקְרִיב תְּמִידִין, וּכְשֶׁמַּאֲכִילוֹ לֶחֶם הוּא כְּמַקְרִיב מְנָחוֹת; וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם רִאשׁוֹן, שֶׁקִּיֵּים כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ קוֹדֶם שֶׁנִּתְּנָה, וּמֵהֵיכָן לָמַד הַתּוֹרָה? אֶלָּא נַעֲשׂוּ שְׁתֵּי כִלְיוֹתָיו כְּמִין שְׁנֵי רַבָּנִים וְהָיוּ נוֹבְעוֹת וּמְלַמְּדוֹת אוֹתוֹ תּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא), וְהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם רִאשׁוֹן; וּכְשֶׁהֶאֱכִילוֹ שָׁם רָמַז לוֹ עַל הַמְּנָחוֹת וְהַנְּסָכִים.
records.originEnglish: The reason is that even this wine was wine used for a mitzvah. Rashi, citing an aggadic midrash, explains that he alluded to the meal offerings and the libations. This follows what is stated in Yoma: “One who wishes to pour wine upon the altar should fill the throats of Torah scholars with wine”; and in Berakhot: “One who hosts a Torah scholar,” and so forth, “Scripture accounts it to him as though he offered the daily offerings.” Feeding a Torah scholar meat resembles offering the daily offerings, while feeding him bread resembles offering meal offerings. Abraham our father was the first Torah scholar, who fulfilled the whole Torah before it was given. Where did he learn it? His two kidneys became like two teachers, flowing and teaching him Torah, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah. He was the first Torah scholar; when Shem fed him, he alluded to the meal offerings and the libations.
records.themeTitle: A scholar’s nourishment can have the function of an offering
records.themeSummary: The ois distinguishes Abraham’s not-yet-completed attainment from the mitzvah embodied in Shem’s hospitality. Bread and wine offered to the first Torah scholar can be understood through the altar’s meal offerings and libations.
records.targetHebrew: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה דַּף י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳): שְׁקוּלָה מִיתָתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים כִּשְׂרֵפַת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵינוּ כִּי גּוּפוֹ מַמָּשׁ דֻּגְמַת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵינוּ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְאִם כֵּן הִיא מַאֲכָלוֹ דֻּגְמַת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת מַמָּשׁ שֶׁמַּקְרִיבִין בְּבֵית הַשֵּׁם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשִׁלְהֵי חֲגִיגָה (דַּף כ״ז עַמּוּד א׳): "זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם", דְּשֻׁלְחָנוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הַשָּׁלֵם בָּזֶה כַּמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאִיתָא (יוֹמָא דַּף ע״א עַמּוּד א׳): "הַמְמַלֵּא גְּרוֹנָם שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים יַיִן — כִּמְקְרִיב נְסָכִים" וְאִיתָא (כְּתֻבּוֹת דַּף ק״ה עַמּוּד ב׳): "הַמֵּבִיא דּוֹרוֹן לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם — כְּאִלּוּ הִקְרִיב בִּכּוּרִים", וְהַכֹּל כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
records.targetEnglish: Concerning this they said in Rosh Hashanah that the death of the righteous is equivalent to the burning of the House of our God: his body itself resembles the House of our God, as explained above. If so, his food truly resembles the offerings brought in God’s House. As it is written at the end of Chagigah, “This is the table that is before the Lord”: the table of a person perfected in this respect is like an altar. Yoma states: “One who fills the throats of Torah scholars with wine is like one who offers libations”; and Ketubot states: “One who brings a gift to a Torah scholar is as though he offered first fruits.” It all follows what was explained above.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek supplies the underlying account of the same libation saying: when a person’s embodied life becomes a dwelling for the Shekhinah, sustaining that life resembles an offering in the Temple. The immediately preceding paragraph defines this through the heart’s continual attachment and the direction of all the limbs. That qualification makes the comparison more than a verbal equivalence between wine and libations, and illuminates why Lech Lecha specifies Abraham’s Torah stature.

records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב: "וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק וְגוֹמֵר הוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיָיִן, וְהוּא כֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן", וְלִכְאוֹרָה הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר: "וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם וְהוּא כֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן הוֹצִיא וְגוֹמֵר"! אַךְ פֵּירוּשׁ הַכָּתוּב "וְהוּא כֹהֵן וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁבִּשְׁעָתָהּ שֶׁהוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיַיִן הָיָה שָׁם כֹּהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן, שֶׁהָיָה הַמְּכֻוָּון שֶׁלּוֹ לְהַקְרִיב לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם לֶחֶם וָיַיִן שֶׁנֶּחְשָׁב כִּמְנָחוֹת וּנְסָכִים, וְהוּא בִּבְחִינַת כֹּהֵן הַמַּקְרִיב.
records.originEnglish: This is what Scripture says: “Melchizedek,” and so forth, “brought out bread and wine, and he was a priest of God Most High.” Seemingly it should have said: “Melchizedek king of Salem, who was a priest of God Most High, brought out,” and so forth! Rather, the meaning of “and he was a priest” is that, at the very time he brought out bread and wine, Shem was a priest of God Most High. His intention was to offer bread and wine to a Torah scholar, which is reckoned as meal offerings and libations; he was thus in the aspect of a priest bringing an offering.
records.themeTitle: The priestly title describes an act of transmitting holiness
records.themeSummary: The placement of “he was a priest” after the bread and wine makes the title describe Shem’s act of service. The ois reads the hospitality as an offering directed toward Abraham’s Torah stature.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 32:2
records.targetHebrew: "כֹּהֵן" הוּא שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ נִשְׁפָּעִים כָּל הַטּוֹבוֹת וְכָל הַהַשְׁפָּעוֹת; וְלָכֵן כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָה מַלְכִּי צֶדֶק שֶׁעַתָּה הוּא אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ הַנִּבְחָר לְשָׁרֵת לַה', שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ יֵלְכוּ הַהַשְׁפָּעוֹת – הוֹצִיא לֶחֶם וָיָיִן, לְרַמֵּז לוֹ שֶׁעַתָּה הוּא אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ כְּלַל הַהַשְׁפָּעוֹת וְהַצִּנּוֹר; שֶׁכֵּן לֶחֶם וָיַיִן הֵם כְּלַל כָּל הַהַשְׁפָּעוֹת:
records.targetEnglish: A “priest” is one through whom all good things and all influences flow. Therefore, when Melchizedek saw that Abraham our father was now the one chosen to serve God, through whom the influences would pass, he brought out bread and wine. He thereby indicated to him that Abraham our father was now the totality of the influences and their channel, for bread and wine encompass all the influences.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov likewise reads the bread and wine as enacting a priestly function. It explains that function as recognizing and conveying the channel of divine good through Abraham. Lech Lecha emphasizes Shem as the one offering food to a scholar, while Beit Yaakov emphasizes Abraham as the channel being recognized; together they illuminate why the verse’s priestly title belongs to this transaction.

records.originHebrew: אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת, גָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם הָיָה לְטוֹבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהָיָה הֲכָנָה לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת ה עַמּוּד א): "שָׁלֹשׁ מַתָּנוֹת טוֹבוֹת נָתַן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכוּלָּן לֹא נְתָנָן אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, וְאֵלּוּ הֵן: תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי", וְעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין שֶׁבְּגָלוּת מִצְרַיִם זָכוּ לַתּוֹרָה. אַךְ הַפֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – שֶׁהוֹדִיעוּהוּ גָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם, וְעַבְדוּת "וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אֹתָם", וְעַל זֶה הָעוֹנֶשׁ נֶחְלְקוּ בַּגְּמָרָא בְּטַעֲמוֹ.
records.originEnglish: In truth, the Egyptian exile was for Israel’s good, as preparation for receiving Torah. As stated in Berakhot: “The Holy One, blessed be He, gave Israel three good gifts, and gave all of them only through afflictions: Torah,” and so forth. Through the afflictions of the Egyptian exile they merited Torah. The meaning of Abraham our father’s punishment is that he was informed of the Egyptian exile and the servitude, “They will serve them and afflict them.” The Talmud disputes the reason for this punishment.
records.themeTitle: Exile makes a prior bond recognizable through service
records.themeSummary: The paragraph distinguishes Israel’s preparation for Torah from Abraham’s painful foreknowledge. The question is what the exile prepared, without turning Israel’s suffering into punishment for an act attributed to Abraham.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 27:4

records.targetEnglish: “This bitter herb that we eat,” and so forth, “because the Egyptians embittered our ancestors’ lives.” The matter of bitter herbs is like what we find in the holy Zohar: had Israel not descended to Egypt and been refined there, they would not have been His unique people. How can this be understood? It is written, “When the Most High allotted nations,” and “For the Lord’s portion is His people”; Israel was already the Lord’s portion from the generation of the Dispersion. The matter is that Israel was then also His portion, but only by the lot—that is, from the side of the blessed God. In Egypt, through the action of their service, Israel was clarified as being His portion. This is “Had they not descended to Egypt”: they were there under intense concealment, as it is written, “You know how we lived in the land of Egypt,” and “You saw their abominations and their idols.” Nevertheless, they had the power to restrain themselves. This clarified that they were “Jacob, the cord of His inheritance”: through their service they have a line and cord, showing that they are the Holy One’s portion and lot. Through their service they recognize the line and cord by which they are bound to the root, as it is written, “To know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you.” This recognition is possible only through the intense concealment that came before.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives a specific account of preparation in Egypt: a bond already present from God’s side becomes something Israel can recognize through its own restrained service under concealment. That helps explain how Lech Lecha can call the exile preparation for a gift. Its focus is the formation of recognition and service, not a new reason to blame Israel for Abraham’s conduct.

records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁהוֹדִיעוּהוּ בְּכָאן גָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם, וּבַסּוֹף: "וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן יֵצְאוּ בִּרְכוּשׁ גָּדוֹל", וְ"גָדוֹל" מוֹרֶה עַל מִדּוֹת עַתִּיקָא, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁמְּקֻשָּׁרִין בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ, וְזֶה הָרְכוּשׁ גָּדוֹל שֶׁהוֹצִיאוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם, שֶׁנִּתְבָּרְרוּ שָׁם עַל יְדֵי הָעֶשֶׂר מַכּוֹת בְּכָל הָעֶשֶׂר מִדּוֹת, שֶׁבְּכָל מַכָּה יָצְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּדָּה אַחַת בַּקְּלִיפָּה, שֶׁיֵּשׁ גַּם כֵּן עֶשֶׂר זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה, וְנִכְנְסוּ בִּקְדוּשָׁה בְּמִדָּה אַחַת, עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב, לו עַמּוּד א): "נָגוֹף לְמִצְרַיִם וְרָפוֹא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל".
records.originEnglish: This is why he was informed here of the Egyptian exile and, at its end, “Afterward they will go out with great possessions.” “Great” indicates the qualities of Atika: being bound to the root. These are the great possessions they brought out of Egypt. Through the ten plagues they were clarified there in all ten qualities: in each plague Israel left one quality on the impure side, which also has ten corresponding qualities, and entered one quality in holiness. This resembles the holy Zohar’s expression, “Striking Egypt and healing Israel.”
records.themeTitle: The great possessions are capacities redirected toward holiness
records.themeSummary: The promise of wealth is interpreted through the ten plagues as a passage out of opposing qualities and into holiness. Its greatness concerns connection to the root, not only the quantity of material property.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה טַעַם שֶׁקִּבֵּל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מַתָּנוֹת מִמִּצְרַיִם, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה לִשְׁתֵּי כִלְיוֹתָיו כִּשְׁנֵי רַבָּנִים וְהָיוּ מְלַמְּדִין אוֹתוֹ חָכְמָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סא), שֶׁקָּלַט הַחֵשֶׁק לְחָכְמָה שֶׁלָּהֶם, רַק שֶׁהוּא חָשַׁק לְחָכְמַת אֱמֶת. וְכָךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קִבֵּל רוּחַ חָכְמָה וּבִינָה מִמִּצְרַיִם, וְרוּחַ עֵצָה וּגְבוּרָה מֵאֲבִימֶלֶךְ; וְשֶׁזֶּה טַעַם שֶׁאָמְרוּ: מֵאֲבִימֶלֶךְ נִתְעַבְּרָה שָׂרָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תּוֹלְדוֹת), כִּי בְּעֵת שֶׁנִּיטַּל כֹּחַ הַהוֹלָדָה מֵאֲבִימֶלֶךְ, אָז נִיתַּן כֹּחוֹ לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.  וְזֶה עִנְיַן הַבְטָחַת: "יֵצְאוּ בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל" (בְּרֵאשִׁית טו, יד) וּבִזַּת הַיָּם, וְהוּא הֲכָנָה לְחָכְמַת הַתּוֹרָה. רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם שָׁרְשׁוֹ מִצַּד חָכְמַת חִיצוֹנוֹת; וּבִשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶאֱמַר: "וַתֵּרֶב חָכְמַת וְגוֹמֵר וּמִכָּל חָכְמַת מִצְרָיִם" (מְלָכִים א ה, י), דְּהַיְינוּ בְּחָכְמַת חִיצוֹנוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם. וְכָל חֵשֶׁק שְׁלֹמֹה הָיָה לְחָכְמָה, שֶׁעַל זֶה בִּיקֵּשׁ בַּחֲלוֹם רַק זֶה. וְכָךְ כֹּחוֹ קָבוּעַ בָּרְכוּשׁ, וּלְזֶה חָשַׁק שִׁישַׁק, וְחָזַר לִמְקוֹמוֹ; כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת חָכְמַת חִיצוֹנוֹת הוּא חֶלְקָם, רַק שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁאֵלָה לְשָׁעָה לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְצוֹרֶךְ לִקְבּוֹעַ בְּלִבָּם עַל יְדֵי זֶה חָכְמַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְעַד שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁחִבֵּר מִשְׁלֵי בְּבֵירוּר חָכְמַת הַתּוֹרָה, וְאָז לֹא הוּצְרְכוּ עוֹד לְחָכְמַת חִיצוֹנוֹת, וְחָזַר כָּל אֶחָד לִמְקוֹמוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: This is why Abraham our father accepted gifts from Egypt. Through them he merited that his two kidneys were like two teachers, teaching him wisdom, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah: he absorbed their desire for wisdom, but his desire was for true wisdom. I similarly heard that Abraham our father received a spirit of wisdom and understanding from Egypt, and a spirit of counsel and might from Abimelech. This explains [the scoffers’] claim that Sarah became pregnant from Abimelech: when the power of procreation was taken from Abimelech, his power was given to Abraham our father. This is the promise, “They will go out with great possessions,” and the spoils of the sea: preparation for the wisdom of Torah. Nevertheless, its root lay in external wisdom. Of Solomon it is said that his wisdom exceeded all the wisdom of Egypt—that is, their external wisdom. Solomon’s entire desire was for wisdom, and in his dream he asked only for this. His power was likewise fixed in his possessions; Shishak desired this, and it returned to its place. External wisdom was truly their portion, but it was lent temporarily to Israel so that through it the wisdom of the blessed God could be established in their hearts. This continued until King Solomon, who composed Proverbs to clarify the wisdom of Torah. Then they no longer needed external wisdom, and each thing returned to its place.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains how possessions can bear a people’s cultivated desire and capacity. Abraham receives the Egyptian desire for wisdom but directs it toward truth; the later “great possessions” likewise prepare for Torah. This supplies a concrete example of the transfer from an opposing quality into holiness described in Lech Lecha. Its qualification is preserved: the external wisdom serves a temporary preparatory purpose and is not equated with Torah itself.

records.originHebrew: וְכֵן מָצִינוּ שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אַרְבַּע כּוֹסוֹת בְּפֶסַח, אַף שֶׁהוּא שִׁיעוּר שִׁכְרוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ (כְּתוּבּוֹת סה עַמּוּד א): "אַרְבַּע – אֲפִילּוּ חֲמוֹר תּוֹבַעַת וְכוּלֵי", וְלָמָּה תִּקְּנוּ שִׁיעוּר שִׁכְרוּת? אַךְ בִּיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם שֶׁנִּתְבָּרְרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמַכָּה עֲשִׂירִית שֶׁהֵם "בְּנִי בְכֹרִי יִשְׂרָאֵל", וּ"בְנִי" הַיְינוּ שֶׁקָּשׁוּר בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּעוֹלַת תָּמִיד לְהָרַמַּ"ע: "נֶפֶשׁ הָאָב מַזָּל לָבָן", וּמַזָּלָא הַיְינוּ עַתִּיקָא כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, עט עַמּוּד ב), וְלָכֵן בָּאָה הַמִּצְוָה בְּיַיִן בְּשִׁיעוּר שִׁכְרוּת, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן בִּקְדוּשָׁה.
records.originEnglish: We similarly find that our Sages ordained four cups at Passover, even though this is an amount that produces intoxication, as stated in Ketubot: “Four—even a donkey she solicits,” and so forth. Why did they ordain an amount that produces intoxication? At the Exodus, through the tenth plague, Israel was clarified as “My firstborn son, Israel.” “My son” means being bound to the root, as stated in the Rema of Fano’s Olat Tamid: “The father’s soul is the son’s mazal.” Mazal signifies Atika, as stated in the Zohar. Therefore the commandment came through an amount of wine that produces intoxication, which is also in holiness.

records.targetEnglish: Through Shabbat one repairs the past. “It gladdens” means “Joy for the upright of heart”: one merits straightness of heart, so that both hearts are only good, emptying the evil from the fool’s heart until everything is very good. Therefore, in the passage of the omer, which comes from barley to clarify that even one whose actions resemble an animal’s is nevertheless intended to become “very good”—light emerging from darkness—this festival is specifically called simply “Shabbat.” Wine in an amount that produces intoxication also occurs in it, to clarify Israel, who is recognized through his cup: in Israel [wine] is “If he merits, it gladdens him,” as stated in Yoma, for he merits straightness of heart. As we have said, eating on this festival comes in holiness, with the blessing “Who sanctified us through His commandments.” It repairs the root of the damage that occurred through eating, when the curse was “You shall eat the plants of the field.” The changed practice of dipping vegetables addresses this, which was a cause of “They embittered their lives with hard labor.” Afterward comes the commandment of eating matzah, nullifying the leaven in the dough. We recite “Who sanctified us through His commandments” over these acts of eating; this itself brings holiness to Israel, and through it all the eating of the entire year is repaired to be in holiness.
records.explanation: The Pesach discourse explains the active repair accompanying the disclosed bond: commanded eating and wine can straighten the heart and turn a damaged past toward holiness. Its discussion of the cup is thus joined to matzah and the blessings of sanctification. This develops Lech Lecha’s claim beyond ancestry alone, while preserving the relation between the wine and the particular holy meal in which it is commanded.

records.targetEnglish: He explained the matter: these four cups of Passover allude to the vessel a person prepares from his own side for redemption. Just as the blessed God acts at that time to illuminate salvation for Israel in stages—as in “Then He saw it, recounted it, prepared it, and also examined it,” four stages—so the person is obliged to prepare himself in correspondence with that divine will, to become a vessel for receiving salvation from the blessed God. The principal preparation of the vessel is to illuminate eyes within the kingdom of Heaven, for the kingdom of Heaven has no eyes, and the person must introduce eyes into it. As our Sages said concerning the cup of Kiddush over wine: a person must direct his eyes toward it. That is, he should see within every concealment the truth that the blessed God alone governs there too. Therefore they said: “Wine—some drink it and it is bad for them ... for a Torah scholar it is always good.” Since the Torah scholar can show God’s governance within every forgetting and concealment, he has a vessel for receiving wine, and drinks it to his good.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim adds the recipient’s work to the four-cup symbolism. The human response to the stages of redemption is to become capable of seeing God’s governance within concealment, expressed by attending to the cup. This clarifies why Lech Lecha’s bond to the root is relevant to receiving wine in holiness: the cup belongs to a capacity for recognition, not simply to the volume consumed.

records.originEnglish: Abraham our father, who contained the congregation of Israel within himself—as indicated by “I will make you a great nation”—also merited the quality of greatness; the word “great” reaches to the root. But he merited this only afterward, when he had entered his days and was called a native within Israel. Here, before circumcision, he had not yet merited it and had not yet merited the quality of “in all.” He was therefore informed that his children would be enslaved in Egypt before they merited the great possessions. This is Rabbi Levi’s intention in saying, “We have not come away empty from this”: he was told, “They will serve them,” and so forth, and he was not yet fit for wine.
records.themeTitle: A promised root becomes settled through successive days of service
records.themeSummary: The conclusion maintains the difference between Abraham’s inclusive root and the attainment he reached only afterward. The timing of “entering his days” matters to the interpretation of the wine.
records.targetHebrew: היינו שקבע השי"ת את עבודת אאע"ה שהיה עובד בכל יום וביום מחרתו נתעלם מאתו עבודתו מיום אתמול כי נקבע בלבו בקביעות גמור ונעשה אצלו כמו לבוש וכן כל העבודות של אאע"ה שהיו אצלו דבר יום ביומו נעשה מהם לבושין ואח"כ ביום מחרתו התחיל אצלו סדר חדש מעבודה ומאותו ההעלם שנתעלמה ממנו עבודת אתמול ונעשה ממנה יומין עלאין יומין ידיעאן ברזא דמהימנותא. מהם נבנה עיקר בנין עולם כי העולם נקרא על שם העלם כדכתיב גם את העלם נתן בלבם וגו' ועל זה כתיב זכרתי לך חסד נעוריך אהבת כלולותיך לכתך אחרי וגו' היינו כי ע"י שנתעלמו עבודות אדם ונקבעו אצלו בתוך לבושי עוה"ז נמצא שהאדם נמשך אח"כ עם כל הלבושים שלו גם בלא דעתו אחר רצונו ית' וזה נקרא לכתך אחרי
records.targetEnglish: The blessed God fixed the service Abraham our father performed each day. On the following day, the previous day’s service became concealed from him because it had been fixed completely within his heart and had become like a garment for him. Thus all Abraham’s acts of service, each in its day, became garments; afterward, on the following day, a new order of service began for him. From that concealment, in which yesterday’s service became hidden and became “supernal days, days known through the mystery of faith,” the principal building of the world was formed. The world is called olam from he’elem, concealment, as it is written, “He also placed the olam in their hearts.” Of this it is written: “I remember for you the kindness of your youth, the love of your bridal days, your following after Me.” As a person’s acts of service become concealed and fixed within the garments of this world, the person is afterward drawn, with all his garments, after God’s will even without his conscious knowledge. This is called “your following after Me.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains “entering his days” as the establishment of earlier service within the person, so that it continues to direct embodied life while a new stage of work begins. This gives a mechanism for Lech Lecha’s distinction between the greatness present in Abraham’s root and its later settled attainment. It does not treat the original promise as proof that every later capacity was already actual.

records.originHebrew: וְצָרִיךְ לְהָבִין, לָמָּה נָטַע נֹחַ הַכֶּרֶם בַּתְּחִלָּה? וְאַף לְמַאן דְּאָמַר עֲנָבִים סְחָטָהּ וְנָתְנָה לוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם, אַחַר שֶׁרָאָה הַקִּלְקוּל בְּוַדַּאי אַחַר זֶה נִזְהַר כָּל יָמָיו וְלֹא שָׁתָה עוֹד יַיִן וְלֹא סָחַט עֲנָבִים, וּבְוַדַּאי כֵּן הָיָה עַד נֹחַ, כְּמַשְׁמָעוּת לְשׁוֹן "וַיָּחֶל נֹחַ" שֶׁהָיָה הָרִאשׁוֹן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב מַהַרְשָׁ"א; וּמֵאֵיזוֹ סִבָּה עָלָה עַל דַּעַת נֹחַ לִיטַּע כֶּרֶם וְלִשְׁתּוֹת יַיִן?
records.originEnglish: One must understand: why did Noah first plant the vineyard? Even according to the view that Eve squeezed grapes and gave them to Adam, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah, after he saw the damage he surely took care for the rest of his life and no longer drank wine or squeezed grapes. Surely this continued until Noah, as the expression “Noah began” implies—that he was the first, as the Maharsha writes. What, then, caused Noah to think of planting a vineyard and drinking wine?
records.themeTitle: Noah’s vineyard was an attempted spiritual repair
records.themeSummary: The opening question concerns Noah’s reason for choosing wine despite the earlier failure. The ois eventually explains his inference from the permission to eat meat, while distinguishing that inference from an effective form of sanctification.
records.targetHebrew: וּלְכָךְ נֹחַ נָטַע כֶּרֶם לִגְדּוֹר מִתַּאֲוָה, אֲבָל יַיִן יֵשׁ שׁוֹתֵהוּ וְרַע לוֹ, לַמַּשְׂמְאִילִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; וּלְכָךְ "וַיִּשְׁכַּר וַיִּתְגַּל" בְּרֵאשִׁית ט, כא יָצָא מִגֶּדֶר הַצְּנִיעוּת וְהַהַגְדָּרָה הָרְאוּיָה בְּהֶצְנֵעַ כְּמוֹ בְּשָׁאוּל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אוֹת יג דִּכְשֶׁאֵינוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, אַף שֶׁמּוּגְדָּר – כְּאֵינוֹ מוּגְדָּר.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore Noah planted a vineyard to set a boundary against desire. But “Wine—some drink it and it is bad for them,” for those who turn to its left, as explained above. Therefore “He became intoxicated and uncovered himself”: he departed from the boundary of modesty and from the restraint that should be held in concealment, as with Saul. As I wrote above, when it is not for the sake of Heaven, even someone who is restrained is as though he were unrestrained.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explicitly identifies a purpose beyond pleasure in Noah’s planting: he sought to set a boundary against desire. This makes the question at the beginning of Lech Lecha intelligible without treating Noah as simply ignoring Adam’s failure. It also explains why the intended repair can fail: a form of restraint does not by itself establish that the act is directed to Heaven.

records.originHebrew: אַךְ הָעִנְיָן, דִּלְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן לֹא הוּתַּר לֶאֱכֹל מִן הַחַי, וְאַף קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל כְּתִיב: "הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי לָכֶם אֶת כָּל עֵשֶׂב וְגוֹמֵר לָכֶם יִהְיֶה לְאָכְלָה", וּלְנֹחַ נֶאֱמַר: "כָּל רֶמֶשׂ אֲשֶׁר הוּא חַי לָכֶם יִהְיֶה לְאָכְלָה וְגוֹמֵר". וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ (פט עַמּוּד ב) אִיתָא בְּטַעַם קָרְבַּן בְּהֵמָה: "מַה חָטָאת וְכוּלֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּחָטָא וְכוּלֵי, וּלְבָתַר אָתָא נֹחַ וְחָמָא דְּהָא גוּפָא אִתְבְּנֵי מֵאַתְרָא דְּיֵצֶר הָרָע אִקְרִיב קָרְבָּנָא וְכוּלֵי; אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: מִכָּאן וּלְהָלְאָה, הוֹאִיל וְגוּפָא אִשְׁתָּאִיב מֵהַהוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע, יִתְעַנַּג גּוּפָא כְּמָה דְּאִתְחֲזֵי לֵיהּ, יֵיכוֹל בִּשְׂרָא וְכוּלֵי; וּמֵהַהוּא עֹנֶג גּוּפָא חָטָא בְּכַמָּה חֲטָאִין; אָמַר קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא: כַּפָּרָה עַל גּוּפָא בִּשְׂרָא, בִּשְׂרָא אָכִיל וְכוּלֵי", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
records.originEnglish: The matter is that Adam was not permitted to eat from living creatures. Even before the damage it is written, “Behold, I have given you every plant,” and so forth, “it shall be for you to eat”; whereas Noah was told, “Every moving thing that lives shall be for you to eat.” In the holy Zohar on this portion, in its account of an animal offering, it says: “What sin had [the animal] committed? ... Once he sinned ... afterward Noah came and saw that the body was built from the place of the evil inclination, and he brought an offering. ... The Holy One, blessed be He, said: From now on, since the body has drawn from that evil inclination, let the body enjoy itself as is fitting for it; let it eat meat. ... Through that bodily pleasure it sinned in many sins. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let flesh be an atonement for the body; it ate flesh,” and so forth. Examine the passage there.
records.themeTitle: Repair must reach the embodied place in which the damage occurred
records.themeSummary: The ois introduces the Zohar’s sequence of embodied desire, the permission to eat meat, and an offering of flesh. The following paragraphs ask how such nourishment can produce either repair or a further failure.
records.targetHebrew: היינו כי כיון שחטא באלו הלבושים אמר השי"ת בשרא אכיל והתענג לגופא מבשרא בשרא יהי' לכפרה כי הקנינים של אדם עם האדם לאחדים המה לכן כיון שהכניס אדם א"ע למקום החושך צריך דווקא האדם בבחירת דעתו להאיר שם ולברר הטוב מן הרע ולהאיר הכ"ש בכל הלבושים שלו כי מאחר שרואה האדם נגדו חושך יכול לפשוט מזה שיכול לחפור ע"י עבודתו בזה החושך בעצמו את האור כי כל החושך הוא רק ממה שעמלק מכסה את אור הפנים וכאשר רואים את המכסה המסתיר יכולין להוכיח שתחת המכסה יש אור בהיר:
records.targetEnglish: Since he sinned through these garments, the blessed God said: he ate flesh and gave his body pleasure through flesh; let flesh be for atonement. A person’s possessions and the person himself form a unity. Therefore, since a person brought himself into a place of darkness, the person must specifically, through the choice of his understanding, illuminate there, separate the good from the evil, and make the glory of Heaven shine within all his garments. Since a person sees darkness before him, he can infer that through his service he can uncover the light within that very darkness. All the darkness comes only from Amalek’s covering the light of the face; when one sees the concealing cover, one can infer that beneath the cover there is brilliant light.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim comments on the same Zohar passage and explains why the repair uses the embodied domain of the failure. Because the person and his possessions have become connected, chosen service must illuminate those very garments. This supplies the mechanism behind Lech Lecha’s difficult sequence of flesh, pleasure, and flesh as atonement; it does not remove the danger that the next paragraphs attribute to eating without holiness.

records.originHebrew: וְנִרְאֶה מִדִּבְרֵי הַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ דַּאֲכִילַת הַבָּשָׂר גּוֹרֵם קִטְרוּג הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְגוֹרֵם לַחֲטוֹא, וְאִם כֵּן אַדְּרַבָּה תִּקְשֶׁה, לָמָּה הוּתַּר לְנֹחַ אֲכִילַת הַבָּשָׂר? וְנִרְאֶה כַּוָּנַת הַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ דְּמַיְיתֵי פָּסוּק: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו", וְהוּא דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁזֶּה עִנְיָן עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁמִּתְּחִלָּה נֶאֱמַר: "וְכָל יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ רַק רַע כָּל הַיּוֹם, וַיִּנָּחֶם ה' וְגוֹמֵר", וְגָרַם זֶה מִשְׁפַּט הַמַּבּוּל; וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּתִיב: "לֹא אֹסִף לְקַלֵּל וְגוֹמֵר כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו", וְהָיָה זֶה עַצְמוֹ לִימּוּד זְכוּת שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא עוֹד הַשְׁחָתָה וּמַבּוּל, וְלָכֵן הִתִּיר הַבָּשָׂר כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִימּוּד זְכוּת.
records.originEnglish: The words of the holy Zohar appear to say that eating meat brings the accusation of the evil inclination and causes sin. If so, the question is stronger: why was Noah permitted to eat meat? It appears that the Zohar’s intention in citing “For the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth” is as follows. This very matter was first stated as “Every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day,” followed by “The Lord regretted,” and it caused the judgment of the Flood. Afterward, however, it is written, “I will not again curse,” and so forth, “for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth.” That same fact became a plea in his favor, so that destruction and a flood would not come again. He therefore permitted meat so that there would be a plea in his favor.
records.themeTitle: The same human frailty can become a plea for mercy
records.themeSummary: The ois confronts the use of the heart’s evil inclination first as a reason for judgment and then as a reason to spare the world. Its reading of the permission to eat meat preserves this change in the treatment of embodied frailty.
records.targetHebrew: וְכֵן הָיָה בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל: אַחַר שֶׁלֹּא הִתְפַּלֵּל נֹחַ עַל הַדּוֹר, אַחַר כָּךְ נִשְׁבַּע הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: לֹא אֹסִף לְקַלֵּל עוֹד אֶת הָאֲדָמָה בַּעֲבוּר הָאָדָם, כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו". וְאַף שֶׁזֶּה עַצְמוֹ הָיָה הַטַּעַם שֶׁהֵבִיא הַמַּבּוּל, דִּכְתִיב (שָׁם ו, ה): "וְכָל יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ רַק רַע כָּל הַיּוֹם", לִמֵּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּזֶה עַצְמוֹ זְכוּת עַל הָאָדָם, וְהוּא שֶׁהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע הוּא מִשֶּׁנִּנְעַר לָצֵאת מִמְּעֵי אִמּוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ה) וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (לד, י). וְהוּא לִימּוּד זְכוּת כְּעֵין לִימּוּד זְכוּת מִפָּסוּק "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" שֶׁבַּגְּמָרָא (בְּרָכוֹת לב:).
records.targetEnglish: This also occurred in the generation of the Flood: after Noah did not pray for the generation, the blessed God afterward swore, “I will not again curse the ground because of the human being, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth.” Although this itself had been the reason for bringing the Flood, as it is written, “Every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day,” the blessed God used this very fact as a plea in the human being’s favor. The evil inclination is present from when he stirs to emerge from his mother’s womb, as expounded in the Jerusalem Talmud and Bereishit Rabbah. This is a plea resembling the plea drawn in Berakhot from the verse “Whom I afflicted” [invoked there concerning God’s part in the conditions of wrongdoing].
records.explanation: The Noach discourse specifies the force of “from his youth”: the inclination is already present when the person comes into the world. This gives content to the plea in Lech Lecha rather than merely repeating that God changed from judgment to mercy. The bracketed gloss distinguishes the biblical wording of “Whom I afflicted” from the use to which the author puts that verse.

records.originEnglish: The words of the holy Zohar appear to say that eating meat brings the accusation of the evil inclination and causes sin. If so, the question is stronger: why was Noah permitted to eat meat? It appears that the Zohar’s intention in citing “For the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth” is as follows. This very matter was first stated as “Every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day,” followed by “The Lord regretted,” and it caused the judgment of the Flood. Afterward, however, it is written, “I will not again curse,” and so forth, “for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth.” That same fact became a plea in his favor, so that destruction and a flood would not come again. He therefore permitted meat so that there would be a plea in his favor.
records.themeTitle: The same human frailty can become a plea for mercy
records.themeSummary: The ois confronts the use of the heart’s evil inclination first as a reason for judgment and then as a reason to spare the world. Its reading of the permission to eat meat preserves this change in the treatment of embodied frailty.

records.targetEnglish: “The Lord said to His heart: I will not again curse the ground because of,” and so forth. This thought of the blessed God became known to Noah because, after the Flood, great fear was impressed within his heart: it is not right for a person to give himself free expansion according to his will; he must hold back his spirit. From this he understood that the blessed God’s will likewise was not to curse the ground again.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains how Noah could recognize the new promise: the Flood had impressed restraint upon his own heart. This contributes the human change alongside Lech Lecha’s plea drawn from human frailty. records.originEnglish: In truth, concerning meat too we find: “There is no joy except with meat.” This means meriting straightness of heart, as it is said, “Joy for the upright of heart.” After the damage, meat is needed because there are more holy sparks to bring out from meat than from plants. Thus the Ari explains Rav Chisda’s statement in Shabbat: “In my wealth I did not eat vegetables, for I said: where vegetables would enter, let meat and fish enter.” God forbid that his meaning was to choose meat and fish for pleasure. Rather, “in my wealth” means when he became a Torah scholar and meat was permitted to him, since an unlearned person is forbidden to eat meat, as stated in Pesachim. He then did not eat vegetables because there are more holy sparks to bring out from animals than from plants; therefore he said, “Where vegetables would enter, let meat and fish enter.” This is the end of that explanation. This is also the meaning of their saying in Berakhot: “Every living thing restores the soul, and whatever is near the soul restores the soul”: it too means that there are more holy sparks in it.
records.themeTitle: Animal nourishment requires a power that can transform its vitality
records.themeSummary: The paragraph explains the scholar’s choice of meat through the work carried by that nourishment. “Wealth” here includes Torah stature, and the greater number of sparks is a responsibility to elevate rather than a justification based on stronger pleasure.

records.targetEnglish: An unlearned person is forbidden, for he may become submerged, so that “one kind finds its own kind and is awakened.” But a Torah scholar, even if he is not cleansed in the chambers of his heart, nevertheless already has an advantage over the animal through his wisdom. Through his thought in words of Torah he therefore brings the power of that soul out of its clothing in an animal soul and animal power. Just as, in actuality, the animal’s flesh is transformed to nourish his body and become human flesh, so, in its power, animal power is transformed into human power. This is the reason for the Zohar’s statement, “They are clarified through wisdom.” A Torah scholar can clarify and repair souls even though he is not wholly cleansed of those things himself. Provided that his soul is immersed in words of Torah, through those words he raises and repairs all kinds of foreign thoughts.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains why Torah wisdom matters to the elevation described in Lech Lecha: it can transform animal power into a specifically human power of thought. It carefully distinguishes this capacity from an already flawless heart. The necessary condition is actual immersion in Torah, which makes “more sparks” an account of work to be performed, rather than an automatic benefit of eating meat.

records.targetHebrew: וּלְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹדְעִים שֶׁעִנְיָן זֶה לֹא נִמְצָא בְּיִחוּד רַק בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם בִּלְבַדּוֹ, וּלְזֹאת נִתְרַצּוּ כֻּלָּם לִהְיוֹת לְבָרוּת וּלְמַאֲכָל לְהָאָדָם מִדַּעְתָּם וּמִצִּבְיוֹנָם, בִּכְדֵי שֶׁיִּתְכַּלְּלוּ בְּצוּרַת אָדָם וְיִקְחוּ חֵלֶק בַּעֲבוֹדָתוֹ וּבְכֹחַ בְּחִירָתוֹ שֶׁמְּבָרֵר עַצְמוֹ בִּיגִיעַ כַּפַּיִם.
records.targetEnglish: Since they knew that this matter [service through choice and personal effort] is found distinctively in the human soul alone, they all willingly and freely consented to become nourishment and food for the human being, so that they would be included in the human form and take a share in his service and in the power of his choice, through which he clarifies himself by the labor of his hands.
records.explanation: In its complete account of Noah’s permission to eat meat, Beit Yaakov explains the elevation as animal life taking a share in human service performed through choice. This gives a concrete purpose to the greater vitality Lech Lecha locates in animal food. The bracketed antecedent comes from the preceding discussion; the connection preserves Beit Yaakov’s different framework of willing inclusion rather than attributing Rav Tzadok’s precise account of sparks to it.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Animal life is included in the work of human choice
records.reverseThemeSummary: The complete section explains the permission of meat after the Flood through the recognition of service by human choice and effort. The animal’s inclusion in the human form gives it a share in that work.
records.reverseExplanation: Lech Lecha specifies the kind of spiritual capacity required for such nourishment to serve repair: Torah stature capable of bringing out its holy sparks. Its distinction between a scholar’s purposeful eating and the pursuit of pleasure helps explain why inclusion in the human body is directed toward service, not an end in itself.

records.originHebrew: וְלָכֵן לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל הָיָה דַּי לְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים לְהוֹצִיא הַקְּדוּשָׁה מִן הַצְּמָחִים, וְאַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל צָרִיךְ לַאֲכִילַת הַבָּשָׂר בִּקְדוּשָׁה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי כֵן יִזְכּוּ לְשִׂמְחָה לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֵב אֶחָד לְטוֹב; וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּשֶׁאוֹכֵל הַבָּשָׂר שֶׁלֹּא בִּקְדוּשָׁה, מִסְתַּעֵף מֵאֲכִילַת הַבָּשָׂר קִטְרוּג הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וּבָא לַחֲטָאִים, וְלָכֵן בָּאָה הַכַּפָּרָה בְּדַם הַבְּהֵמָה, "כִּי הַדָּם הוּא בַּנֶּפֶשׁ יְכַפֵּר", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ.
records.originEnglish: Therefore, before the damage, it was sufficient for Adam to sustain life by bringing holiness out of plants. After the damage, eating meat in holiness is needed, so that through it one can merit joy and straighten the heart into one heart for good. Nevertheless, when a person eats meat without holiness, the accusation of the evil inclination branches out from that eating and he comes to sins. Therefore atonement comes through the animal’s blood, “For the blood makes atonement through the soul,” as stated in the holy Zohar.
records.themeTitle: Eating in holiness directs both nourishment and desire toward God
records.themeSummary: The paragraph holds together the possible repair through meat and the risk of further failure through it. The decisive condition is the holiness of the eating, which must affect the heart rather than merely the food consumed.
records.targetHebrew: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: מִשֶּׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ אֵין לוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה; וּכְשֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה שֻׁלְחָנוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה, אָז הוּא נַעֲשָׂה דֻּגְמַת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וּמִזְבֵּחַ, וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא אוֹכֵל הוּא דֻּגְמַת כֹּהֲנִים, "כִּי קָא זָכוּ — מִשֻּׁלְחַן גָּבוֹהַּ קָא זָכוּ"; שֶׁהַחֵלֶב וְהַדָּם, רָצָה לוֹמַר עִקַּר הַחִיּוּת שֶׁבַּמַּאֲכָל וְהַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּאָדָם לוֹ, הוּעֲלָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה (שֶׁנִּמְשְׁלוּ לְאֵשׁ שֶׁהוּא אֵשׁ הַמַּעֲרָכָה), שֶׁמַּכִּיר עַל יָדוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן הַחִיּוּת בַּמַּאֲכָל, וְהַנּוֹתֵן הַתַּאֲוָה לָאָדָם וְהַחֵשֶׁק לְזֶה הַמַּאֲכָל לְקַיֵּם נַפְשׁוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: This comes only through words of Torah, as it is written: since the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has only the four cubits of halakhah. When one’s table becomes four cubits of halakhah, it resembles the Temple and altar, and what one eats resembles the priests’ eating: “When they receive their share, they receive it from the table of the Most High.” The fat and blood—that is, the principal vitality within the food and the person’s desire for it—have been raised to the blessed God through words of Torah, which are compared to fire, the fire of the altar’s arrangement. Through them one recognizes that the blessed God gives vitality to the food and gives the person desire and longing for this food to sustain his soul.
records.explanation: Et HaOchel defines the positive content of “eating in holiness.” Torah at the table directs both the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire to their divine source; its fat-and-blood imagery concerns both sides of the encounter. This explains why Lech Lecha can describe the same embodied nourishment as a means of repair or a cause of further disorder, depending on how it is received.

records.originEnglish: The same applies to wine. Rav Nachman, a son-in-law of the house of the Nasi, said: “The reason I did not tell you in the evening was that I had not eaten ox meat.” Tosafot explain that he had been fasting, and whenever he had not eaten meat, his mind was not settled for Torah. Rav Nachman also said: “Until I have drunk a quarter-log of wine, my mind is not clear.” He was wealthy and needed meat and wine for Torah. But someone who cannot afford them certainly does not need meat and wine. In the Talmudic period they did not ordinarily have meat and wine every day, as we find: “People such as us, for whom meat and wine are available every day”—implying specifically people such as us. This resembles Rabbi Yochanan’s statement: “Abba [Rav] was from a family of healthy people, but people such as us,” and so forth. Rav Nachman likewise said: “People such as us borrow and eat,” meaning that they needed the meat.

records.targetHebrew: וזה דקדוק לשון רש"י ז"ל שלא יתאוה אדם לאכול בשר אלא מתוך רחבת ידים ועושר. עושר כולל ב' כונות עושר ממון היינו כיון שנותן לו השי"ת עושר מן הסתם הבשר הוא לו ללחם חוקו כמו שאמרנו בשלמה המע"ה ובר' נחמן. וגם עושר בד"ת ע"ד שא' (במד"ת תשא ג') על הפ' והשבע לעשיר וגו' בעשירי תורה אני מדבר ולא בעשירי ממון וכו'. וכן נדרש (תמורה ט"ז.) עשיר ורש נפגשו על חכם וטפש. ומי שיש לו עושר בד"ת ובטוח שנצרך לו הבשר לד"ת ג"כ הותר לו הבשר כמו שאמר ר"נ כגון אנו לוין ואוכלין רק רב מחמיר על עצמו היה כמו שאמר ר' יוחנן אבא וכו':
records.targetEnglish: This is the precision of Rashi’s wording: a person should not desire to eat meat except from ample means and wealth. “Wealth” includes two meanings. There is wealth of money: since the blessed God gives him wealth, presumably the meat is his allotted bread, as we explained regarding King Solomon and Rav Nachman. There is also wealth in words of Torah, as they said concerning “The rich person’s satiety”: “I speak of those rich in Torah, not those rich in money,” and so forth. “A rich person and a poor person meet” is likewise expounded regarding a wise person and a fool. Someone who possesses wealth in Torah and is certain that the meat is needed for Torah is also permitted meat, as Rav Nachman said: “People such as us borrow and eat.” Rav, however, was stringent with himself, as Rabbi Yochanan said: “Abba,” and so forth.
records.explanation: The Re’eh discourse explicitly distinguishes financial wealth from wealth in Torah and explains the borrowing case through certainty of a real Torah need. This adds a necessary refinement to the differentiated examples in Lech Lecha: the measure is not a single diet determined by social status. The full target also preserves Rav’s caution about mistaking bodily desire for the soul’s need, so that claimed need is not automatically treated as established.

records.targetHebrew: הענין בזה שהשי"ת אין נותן לאדם כי אם מה שנצרך לשורש נפשו, ואף שרואים איזה פעמים שיש אדם שיש לו רוב טובה שנראה כמותרות, אכן באמת גם זה נצרך לו הכל לשורש החיים, כי באם לא היה נצרך לו לשורש החיים לא היה נותן לו השי"ת. ועל הטובה שנצרך לו לאדם לשורש החיים, השי"ת מעורר לו כח התפלה שיתפלל על זה, ואז השי"ת נותן לו, וזה היה ברבי חנינא בן דוסא, שהיה די לו בקב חרובים, היינו מפני שלא נצרך לו לשורש החיים שלו יותר, רק מה שנחסר לכלל ישראל זה היה חסר לו לשורש החיים, ובעבור זה היה כל העולם ניזון בשבילו.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is that the blessed God gives a person only what is needed for the root of his soul. Even when one sometimes sees a person with an abundance of good that appears superfluous, in truth all of it too is needed for the root of life; had it not been needed, the blessed God would not have given it to him. For the good a person needs at the root of life, the blessed God awakens within him the power of prayer to pray for it, and then gives it to him. This was the case with Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, for whom a kav of carobs was sufficient: he did not need more for the root of his own life. Rather, whatever the entirety of Israel lacked was lacking for him at the root of his life; because of this, the whole world was sustained on his account.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why little food in one righteous life and abundant provision in another need not be contradictory ideals. The provision corresponds to the soul’s actual task and need; Rabbi Chanina’s personal sufficiency also coexists with a need encompassing all Israel. This illuminates Lech Lecha’s repeated “people such as us” without generalizing Rav Nachman’s requirement to every reader.

records.originEnglish: This also explains Noah’s case. After meat was permitted to him, so that through it he could set his heart straight and gladden it, Noah thought that wine was likewise needed to set the heart straight and attain joy. Adam’s situation before the damage, he thought, provided no proof against this. That was his reason for planting a vineyard. In truth, however, the wine that sets the heart straight is only the wine of Kiddush, which is wine used for a mitzvah, or wine needed by someone for the mental composure necessary for Torah. As the holy Zohar says, “Sages who resemble Sabbaths”: all their eating is in holiness, like eating on Shabbat and festivals, for all their eating sustains life for Torah. For them wine is needed as it is on Shabbat, when a person establishes his meal over wine.
records.themeTitle: Joy must come from real clarity rather than imagined completeness
records.themeSummary: Noah’s intention to straighten the heart does not establish that wine will accomplish it. The ois requires a concrete mitzvah or a genuine need for settled Torah understanding; the effect must match the proposed spiritual purpose.
records.targetHebrew: ומפני זה נאסרו אנשי משמר לשתות יין, כי אף שהיין ישמח לבב אנוש, הוא מפני שהוא משכר ומטריד הדעה עד שנראה לו שאינו בעל חסרון והוא שלם בכל, אבל באמת זה עיקר חסרון ואין למעלה ממנו, כשאדם בעל חסרון ומרמה את עצמו שהוא שלם, ומפני זה הכהנים בעת שהיו עומדים על העבודה היו צריכים להיות עומדים בבהירות ובישוב הדעת, כי השי"ת לא יבחר רק בעבודה של ישוב הדעת. ועל זה נאסר להם בעת העבודה שתיית יין שהוא משכר ומטריד הדעת, ואל יעלה על הדעת שהשי"ת רוצה מהאדם שימאס ויבטל לגמרי את עצמו מעניני עוה"ז, כי כל הנבראים לא נבראו לבטלה ח"ו והכל ברא לכבודו, וכל הדברים הם לתועלת האדם לעבודה, ועי"ז יבא האדם להכיר שמלא כל הארץ כבודו. רק זאת רוצה השי"ת מהאדם שעל ידי עניני עוה"ז יבא לעוה"ב, ששם נקרא בי"ה היינו שהשם הוא שלם:
records.targetEnglish: For this reason the members of the priestly watch were forbidden to drink wine. Although wine gladdens the human heart, it does so by intoxicating and disturbing understanding until it seems to the person that he has no lack and is complete in every respect. In truth this is a fundamental lack, with none greater: a person who has a lack deceives himself that he is complete. Therefore, when the priests stood in service, they had to stand in clarity and settled understanding, for the blessed God chooses only service performed with settled understanding. They were therefore forbidden during their service to drink wine that intoxicates and disturbs understanding. Yet it should not occur to one that the blessed God wants a person to reject the affairs of this world and remove himself entirely from them. None of the created things was created in vain, God forbid; He created everything for His glory. All things can benefit a person in service, and through them he will come to recognize that the whole earth is full of His glory. The blessed God wants the person, through the affairs of this world, to come to the world to come, where [the divine name] is read with yod-heh—that is, the Name is complete.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef gives a precise way in which the intended joy can fail: wine can simulate a sense of completeness by disturbing understanding, while the service itself requires clarity. Its conclusion preserves the positive purpose of created things, so it does not answer Noah’s failure by declaring bodily life worthless. This deepens Lech Lecha’s requirement that the wine actually serve a mitzvah or settled understanding.

records.targetEnglish: Shemot Rabbah likewise gives the parable of a king with the queen sitting opposite him: one who passes between them incurs death. On Shabbat, the entire day is an aspect of union between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel, which is the union of the Holy One and His Shekhinah. With every mitzvah one says, “For the sake of the union of the Holy One and His Shekhinah.” On Shabbat, because a person is accustomed to work throughout the six weekdays and rests on Shabbat, the entire day is like encountering a transgression and being spared it, which is reckoned as performing a mitzvah. Through this, the whole day is the union of the Holy One and His Shekhinah through the commandment of Shabbat, since one could easily come to desecrate it through sorting and other easily performed labors. Therefore, throughout the day the Holy One and the congregation of Israel are like the seated king and the queen sitting opposite him; hence a non-Jew who observes such a rest is liable. This is “Come, bride,” the Shabbat queen; in any event, Israel is its partner.
records.explanation: The Pinchas discourse explains the king-and-queen image through the continuous mitzvah of resting from familiar weekday work. The bond is enacted throughout the day, even where no separate positive act is visible. This clarifies the particular Shabbat form of service that Lech Lecha says Noah could not simply assume as the basis for sanctifying his wine.

records.targetHebrew: ובאמת עיקר כח האדם, שיכול להכניס קדושתו על כל פעולותיו, נמשך הכל יען אשר נשרש בו קדושה בקביעות משורש קדושת אבות, ומזה הכח קדושה יכול להכניס גם בכלי פעולותיו, וכעין דאיתא בזוה"ק (תרומה קל"ה) אנן נוטלין מתושב"כ תושבע"פ וכן מקדושת שבת קדושת יו"ט. כי קדושת שבת קבוע וקיימא מצד השי"ת, כי אצל שבת כתיב (שמות כ״ג:י״ב) וביום השביעי תשבות, שזה מורה שמכיר האדם אז שאין לו שום כח פעולה. ואף שבאמת בעוה"ז נדמה לאדם שבת הוא צמצום גדול, כי בחול מכין אדם לעצמו כל צרכי אוכל נפש לחם לאכול ובגד ללבוש ובשבת אסור הכל, ונדמה לאדם בעוה"ז שהוא צמצום גדול, אבל בעומק מרמז שבת ליום שכולו שבת ומנוחה לחיי העולמים. כי שבת מרמז כמו שאיתא בש"ס (שבת ל':) עתידה ארץ ישראל שתוציא גלוסקאות וכלי מילת. והיינו שלא יוצרך האדם לכלי פעולותיו, כי על שבת איתא בזוה"ק (בשלח ס"ג:) מניה מתברכין יומין עילאין. והיינו, שבשורש מקבל האדם אז כח עבודה על כל ששת ימי המעשה.
records.targetEnglish: In truth, the principal power a person has to introduce holiness into all his actions is drawn entirely from the holiness fixed within him at the root of the patriarchs’ holiness. From that holy power he can introduce holiness into the instruments of his actions too. This resembles the holy Zohar’s statement: we take the Oral Torah from the Written Torah, and likewise the holiness of festivals from the holiness of Shabbat. Shabbat’s holiness is fixed and enduring from the side of the blessed God, for concerning Shabbat it is written, “On the seventh day you shall rest.” This indicates that a person then recognizes that he has no independent power of action. Although in this world Shabbat seems a great restriction—for during the week a person prepares all his food and clothing, while on Shabbat it is all forbidden—at its depth Shabbat alludes to the day that is entirely Shabbat and rest for everlasting life. It alludes to the saying that in the future the Land of Israel will produce ready-made loaves and fine garments: the person will not need the instruments of his action. For concerning Shabbat the holy Zohar says: “From it the supernal days are blessed.” This means that, at the root, a person then receives the power of service for all six weekdays.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains how inherited, fixed holiness can become effective in the person’s limbs and actions. Shabbat is the source from which that holiness is drawn, even though its rest can appear merely restrictive. This supplies the positive mechanism behind Lech Lecha’s boundary: sanctification of embodied activity depends on an established root, rather than only on the desire to achieve a future repair.

records.originEnglish: This is “Go for yourself”—to put yourself right, to put your own level right. records.targetHebrew: וְעִנְיַן הַיִּחוּדִים הוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "וּכְשֶׁאַתֶּם מִתְפַּלְּלִין דְּעוּ לִפְנֵי מִי אַתֶּם מִתְפַּלְּלִין" (שָׁם כ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳), וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי הַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת בְּיִחוּדוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁקְּרָאוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה "קַבָּלַת מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם", כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; וְכָל אֵלּוּ דְּבָרִים יְדוּעִים וְלֹא נֶעֶלְמוּ מֵהָרַב יִצְחָק בַּר שֵׁשֶׁת, וְהֵם חוֹבָה לְכָל אָדָם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא, לְהַעֲמִיק בְּכַוָּנַת הַלֵּב בִּתְפִלָּה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דֶּרֶךְ עֲבוֹדָה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלֹא יְכַוֵּין לִגְרָמֵיהּ כְּלוּם רַק לִכְבוֹד שָׁמַיִם,
records.targetEnglish: The matter of unifications is what they said: “When you pray, know before whom you pray.” This comes through recognizing that one is as though standing before the King. It is contemplation of His unity, which our Sages called “acceptance of the kingdom of Heaven,” as explained above. All these matters were known and were not hidden from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Sheshet. They are an obligation upon each person according to his condition: to deepen the intention of the heart in prayer so that it is an act of service before the blessed God, intending nothing for oneself but only for the honor of Heaven.
records.explanation: Sefer HaZikhronot explains the inward content of standing before the King: recognition of divine unity becomes an orientation of prayer toward God rather than toward oneself. This clarifies the awe and directed heart required by Lech Lecha’s standing at Shema. The comparison concerns that common inward meaning; Sefer HaZikhronot is explaining prayer and does not independently establish the rule about walking during Shema.

records.originEnglish: This is “Go for yourself”—to put yourself right, to put your own level right. This is why he cited the rule that, in declaring God’s unity and accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, indicating and recognizing that everything comes from the blessed God, a person must stand and direct his heart to Heaven with dread and awe. When he begins “You shall love,” he may walk if he wishes: in love of the blessed God, the work is to advance from level to level in clarifying oneself. Therefore he may walk or stand according to the state of his service. This is “Go for yourself.”

records.targetEnglish: Accepting the kingdom of Heaven while walking means crowning the blessed God over oneself only outwardly, until one passes through the passage and obtains the desire of one’s heart, after which one will give oneself free expansion in it. They said it is forbidden to act in this way. Rather, acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven must come from the depth of the heart as a fixed commitment; this is what the blessed God desires. If a congregation joins and forms one association with this intention of crowning the one God over themselves, that congregation will possess complete wholeness without division. Even if one states a halakhic teaching and another disagrees and rules the opposite, they are nevertheless joined at the root, where their words contain no division, since their intention is one. As the Talmud says: “Both those who said to kindle and those who said not to kindle intended the same thing”; and “These and those are the words of the living God.”
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov interprets the same standing-and-walking teaching by distinguishing a fixed allegiance from an outward commitment lasting only until a personal aim is obtained. Its account of disagreement rooted in a shared intention shows that fixedness does not require every expression to be identical. This deepens Lech Lecha’s distinction between an unwavering acknowledgment of divine kingship and the varied movement of service.

records.originEnglish: This follows what the Talmud says in Nedarim: at first the Holy One, blessed be He, gave him rule over 243 limbs, and finally over 248. These additional ones are the two eyes, two ears, and the organ of circumcision. Even these organs—his eyes and ears, which are not under his control—would also come under his control, so that he would hear and see only a matter of mitzvah, as the Ran explains.
records.themeTitle: Abraham’s refined perception becomes a source for all Israel
records.themeSummary: The new creation includes faculties that had not been fully subject to Abraham’s voluntary control. The next paragraph explains this as seeing and hearing instruction for service in what he encounters.
records.targetHebrew: ואיפשר לומר שהוא מפני דראובן היה קדושת הראייה לברר ראיית כלל ישראל ושמעון השמיעה לברר שמיעת הכלל שהוא בקדושה. וקדושת כל שבט נכלל בכל כלל ישראל כמ"ש בב"ר ע"פ איש אשר כברכתו ברך אותם. והוא על דרך מ"ש (נדרים לב :) כתיב אברם וכ' אברהם כו' ולבסוף המליכו על רמ"ח איברים אלו הן שתי עינים ושתי אזנים וכו' ופי' הר"ן שהמליכו עליהם שיהיו ברשותו שלא יסתכל ולא ישמע כי אם דבר מצוה. והוא ע"ד מה שנאמר והיה עינך רואות את מוריך. שכל מה שיראה ילמוד ממנו לעבודת השי"ת. וכן וכ' ואזניך תשמענה דבר מאחריך זה הדרך לכו בה. שכל מה שישמע ילמוד ממנו דרך ה'. ועז"נ מכל מלמדי השכלתי שמהכל ישכיל וידע דרך ה' וכולם נקראו מלמדי אף שאינו מכוין ללמדו וזה זכה אברהם אבינו ע"ה אחר המילה (ונת' לך מא' ו) ולכן נתייחס שבט ראובן ושמעון שהם מבררים ראיית ושמיעת כלל ישראל שהוא רק לדבר מצוה כנ"ל.
records.targetEnglish: It may be said that this is because Reuben was the holiness of sight, clarifying the sight of all Israel, and Simeon the holiness of hearing, clarifying the hearing of the whole people in holiness. The holiness of each tribe is included within all Israel, as Bereishit Rabbah explains concerning “He blessed them, each according to his blessing.” This follows what was said in Nedarim: it is written “Abram” and “Abraham,” and finally He gave him rule over 248 limbs, including the two eyes and two ears. The Ran explains that He gave him rule over them so that they would be under his control, seeing and hearing only a matter of mitzvah. This is “Your eyes shall see your teachers”: whatever he sees, he learns from it for the service of the blessed God. Likewise, “Your ears shall hear a word behind you: This is the way; walk in it”: whatever he hears, he learns the way of God from it. Of this it is said, “From all my teachers I gained understanding,” for from everything he gains understanding and knows God’s way. They are all called his teachers even if the other does not intend to teach him. Abraham merited this after circumcision, as explained in Lech Lecha, ois six. Reuben and Simeon were therefore listed in the genealogy, because they clarify the sight and hearing of all Israel solely for a matter of mitzvah.
records.explanation: The Vaera discourse explicitly returns to this ois and explains how Abraham’s attainment reaches beyond the individual patriarch. Reuben and Simeon express the sight and hearing that can be refined throughout Israel, with the holiness of each tribe included in the whole people. This supplies the collective dimension of the “new creation,” rather than merely repeating the number of organs.
