records.originEnglish: Nevertheless, with the blessed God, once He promised “I will make you a great nation,” creating him as a new being, he already merited this immediately. Thus the Ramban writes in the name of Targum Onkelos—although this is absent from the Onkelos before us—that “I will be what I will be” is rendered “I will be with the one with whom I will be.” That is, once the blessed God promises to be with him in the future, He is already with him from the time of the promise. This resembles “I will be gracious to the one to whom I will be gracious” in the future. The name Ehyeh, although it points to the future, nevertheless shines immediately in the present. Likewise, God told him: “I will make you a great nation”—“I will make you,” creating you as a new being, so that the five organs too will be under your control. “A great nation” means that the Israelite nation, bound at the root in the quality of greatness, is included within him; “great” indicates what has no measure, reaching to the root. From this promise Abraham already merited to become a vehicle for the quality of “greatness” and “great.”
records.themeTitle: The future promise gives a present foretaste of its light
records.themeSummary: The ois preserves the later completion at circumcision while explaining an illumination present from the time of the promise. Its account of Ehyeh distinguishes the manifestation of a future bond from the claim that every stage of preparation is already complete.
records.targetHebrew: אך הענין בשאלת מה שמו היינו שכיון שהם ידעו שאינם ראוים עוד לגאולה לפי מעשיהם גם שהוא קודם הזמן כמ"ש (שהש"ר ב) על פי קול דודי הנה זה בא ע"ש. ועל זה ישאלו מה שמו והיינו באיזה מדה ממדותיו יגאלם ועל זה השיבו ה' יתברך שם אהיה אשר אהיה דשם אהיה מורה דאנא זמין כו' ואמר השי"ת למשה אהיה אשר אהיה אהא עם מאן דאהא עם מי שאני עתיד להיות כבר נרגש בהווה ע"ד מה שנאמר וחנותי את אשר אחון (כמשנ"ת פ' לך מא' ו) ועל כן אמר שיאמר להם שם אהיה שמורה על העתיד והיינו התגלות עתיקא שיזכו לזה בשעת קריעת ים סוף כמ"ש בזוהר הקדוש (ח"ב נב ב) וראתה שפחה על הים כו'. וכן במתן תורה דכ' פנים בפנים וגו' חמו ישראל הכא מה דלא חמא יחזקאל כמ"ש (שם פב רע"א) ועל ידי שיאמר להם שם אהיה ירגישו תיכף מעין קדושה זו
records.targetEnglish: Their question “What is His name?” means that they knew their deeds did not yet make them fit for redemption, and that it was also before the time, as stated in Shir HaShirim Rabbah. They would therefore ask: through which of His qualities will He redeem them? The blessed God answered Moses with the name “Ehyeh asher Ehyeh.” Ehyeh signifies “I am destined,” and so forth. The blessed God said: “I will be with the one with whom I will be”—with the one with whom I will be in the future, it is already felt in the present. This resembles “I will be gracious to the one to whom I will be gracious,” as explained in Lech Lecha, ois six. He therefore told him to speak to them the name Ehyeh, indicating the future revelation of Atika that they would merit at the splitting of the sea, as the holy Zohar says concerning the maidservant who saw at the sea. Likewise at the giving of Torah, “Face to face”: Israel saw there what Ezekiel did not see. Through his telling them the name Ehyeh, they would immediately feel a foretaste of that holiness.
records.explanation: Shemot applies the same account of Ehyeh to a concrete question: how can redemption begin before the people’s deeds and the appointed time appear ready? The future revelation gives an initial present foretaste that makes the next step possible. This explains the function of Abraham’s immediate illumination while leaving intact Lech Lecha’s later completion through circumcision and personal refinement.

records.originHebrew: מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל" שֶׁבּוֹרֵא אוֹתוֹ בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה, כְּבָר זָכָה בָּזֶה תֵּיכֶף. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ן זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת) בְּשֵׁם תַּרְגּוּם אוּנְקְלוֹס (וּלְפָנֵינוּ לֵיתָא בְּאוּנְקְלוֹס): תַּרְגּוּם "אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה" – "אֶהֱא עִם מַאן דְּאֶהֱא", עַיֵּין שָׁם; וְהַיְינוּ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַבְטִיחַ שֶׁאֶהְיֶה עִמּוֹ לֶעָתִיד, כְּבָר מֵעֵת הַהַבְטָחָה אֲנִי עִמּוֹ, וְעַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן" לֶעָתִיד; וְשֵׁם אֶהְיֶ"ה, אַף שֶׁמּוֹרֶה עַל הֶעָתִיד, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מוֹפִיעַ תֵּיכֶף בַּהֹוֶה. וְכֵן אָמַר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל" – "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ", שֶׁאֲנִי בּוֹרֵא אוֹתְךָ בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הַחֲמִשָּׁה אֵבָרִים בִּרְשׁוּתְךָ גַּם כֵּן; וְזֶהוּ "לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל", שֶׁהוּא שֶׁנִּכְלַל בּוֹ אֻמָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית שֶׁקְּשׁוּרִים בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ בְּמִדַּת "גָּדוֹל", שֶׁמּוֹרֶה בְּלֹא שִׁיעוּר עַד הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ. וּכְבָר זָכָה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ מֵהַבְטָחָה זוֹ לִהְיוֹת מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת גְּדוּלָּה וְגָדוֹל.
records.originEnglish: Nevertheless, with the blessed God, once He promised “I will make you a great nation,” creating him as a new being, he already merited this immediately. Thus the Ramban writes in the name of Targum Onkelos—although this is absent from the Onkelos before us—that “I will be what I will be” is rendered “I will be with the one with whom I will be.” That is, once the blessed God promises to be with him in the future, He is already with him from the time of the promise. This resembles “I will be gracious to the one to whom I will be gracious” in the future. The name Ehyeh, although it points to the future, nevertheless shines immediately in the present. Likewise, God told him: “I will make you a great nation”—“I will make you,” creating you as a new being, so that the five organs too will be under your control. “A great nation” means that the Israelite nation, bound at the root in the quality of greatness, is included within him; “great” indicates what has no measure, reaching to the root. From this promise Abraham already merited to become a vehicle for the quality of “greatness” and “great.”

records.targetHebrew: ויזרע יצחק בארץ ההוא וימצא בשנה ההוא מאה שערים ויברכהו ה' וגו' (בראשית כ״ו:י״ב). הנה הענין מהזריעה של יצחק אבינו שהכתוב משבח אותה כל כך הוא להורות שיצחק הכיר עוד בההתחלה תיכף בשעת הזריעה כל הצמיחה שיצמח ממנה אח"כ היינו שראה מפורש שאין שם סבלנות גבי ישראל שלא יצמח להם ממנו גודל ישועה כדכתיב אודך ה' כי אנפת בי ישוב אפך ותנחמני כי באמת הוא בעומק הסבלנות בעצמו התחלת הארת הישועה וזהו הענין שכרה דוד שיתין למסקי תהומא כדאיתא בגמרא (סוכה נג:) כי חזי דנחית טובא אמר כמה דמידלי טפי מירטב עלמא וכו' היינו שחפר לעורר מעומק הבירור שיתגלה לעתיד שמעולם לא סבלו ישראל כי לא נפסק מהם שפע אורו ית' בשום פעם וכל הארות הישועה המנהיר עכשיו בזה העולם נמשך רק מלמסקי תהומא שכרה דוד המלך אז וכל הישועות המתהוה לפעמים עכשיו המה רק הארה מהישועה הכוללת שיהיה אי"ה לעתיד לזה מחשב בברכת יצחק כל הישועות סומך נופלים ורופא חולים וגו' ומסיים בתחיית המתים להורות שכל אותן הטובות נצמחים גם עכשיו מגודל הארת הישועה שיהיה לעתיד הנקרא תחיית המתים שמנהיר אז השי"ת מפורש שלא היה מעולם לישראל שום סבלנות כלל ומזה נתעורר לפעמים גם בזה העולם ישועה ולכן היה מחשב יצחק אבינו כל הישועות תיכף משעת הזריעה כי הוא היה רואה כבר הישועה שיהיה לעתיד תיכף בשעת הזריעה עד שהזריעה בעצמה היה נחשב בעיניו ישועה.
records.targetEnglish: “Isaac sowed in that land and found in that year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him.” Scripture praises Isaac’s sowing so greatly to indicate that, at the very beginning, at the time of sowing, he recognized all the growth that would later emerge from it. He saw clearly that no hardship borne by Israel fails to produce a great salvation, as it is written: “I thank You, Lord, that You were angry with me; Your anger will turn away and You will comfort me.” In truth, within the hardship itself lies the beginning of salvation’s illumination. This is the meaning of David digging the channels to raise the deep, as the Talmud says: when he saw that it had descended too far, he said, “The higher it stands, the more it waters the world.” He dug to awaken from the depth of the clarification that will be revealed in the future: that Israel never suffered, for the flow of His light never ceased at any time. All the illuminations of salvation that now shine in this world are drawn from that raising of the deep. The salvations that sometimes occur now are only an illumination of the comprehensive salvation that will be in the future. Therefore Isaac’s blessing enumerates all the salvations—supporting the fallen, healing the sick, and so forth—and concludes with resurrection. All those good things grow even now from the great illumination of the future salvation called resurrection, when the blessed God will show explicitly that Israel never suffered at all. From this a salvation is sometimes awakened in this world too. Isaac therefore reckoned all the salvations from the time of sowing, for he already saw the future salvation then, until the sowing itself was counted as salvation in his eyes.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives a related account of how a future good can already illuminate its beginning: Isaac perceives the later growth within the sowing, and present salvations draw from the comprehensive future one. This gives substance to Lech Lecha’s “shines immediately in the present.” The claim concerns the source and foretaste of the illumination; it does not collapse the lived stages of waiting and refinement.

records.originHebrew: וּמִטַּעַם זֶה פָּתַח בִּמְדְרַשׁ רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ בַּפָּסוּק: "שִׁמְעִי בַת וּרְאִי וְהַטִּי אָזְנֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהוּא נִדְרָשׁ עַל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב גַּם בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא; וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צִוָּה לוֹ שֶׁמִּצִּדּוֹ צָרִיךְ שֶׁיְּבָרֵר עַצְמוֹ בְּמִדָּתוֹ וּבְכָל הַמִּדּוֹת, שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע וְיִרְאֶה רַק עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר לוֹ: "לֶךְ לְךָ" – לְאַתְקָנָא דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ; וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִבְטִיחוֹ בֶּעָתִיד: "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ", שֶׁאֲנִי בּוֹרֵא אוֹתְךָ בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הַחֲמִשָּׁה אֵבָרִים גַּם כֵּן בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ, וְהַיְינוּ אַחַר שֶׁיְּבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּפִי כֹּחוֹ.
records.originEnglish: For this reason the Midrash Rabbah on this portion opens with the verse, “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear.” It is interpreted as referring to Abraham our father, as is also taught in Tanchuma. The blessed God commanded him that, on his own side, he must refine himself in his own quality and in every quality, so that he should hear and see only the service of the blessed God. This is what was said to him: “Go for yourself”—to put your own level right. The blessed God promised him for the future, “I will make you”: I will create you as a new being, so that the five organs too will be under his control. This comes after he has refined himself according to his capacity.
records.themeTitle: Divine completion follows the full use of human capacity
records.themeSummary: The ois holds human refinement and the promised new creation in sequence. The promise of faculties beyond ordinary control does not remove the work entrusted to Abraham within his present power.

records.targetHebrew: וְהָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה הוּא: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת נִמְצָא בְּזֶה הַמָּקוֹם הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת וְשִׁכְחָה וְהֶעְלֵם הַגָּדוֹל עַד מְאֹד, עַד הֵיכָן שֶׁאַף אָדָם צַדִּיק לִפְעָמִים יוּלַּד מִמֶּנּוּ אָדָם רָשָׁע; וְהָעֵצָה הַיְּעוּצָה לָאָדָם לְטוֹב לוֹ אַף בָּזֶה הוּא שֶׁיַּזְעִיר וִיצַמְצֵם הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה כְּפִי כֹּחוֹ, וְאָז יוּכַל לוֹמַר: "לֵךְ לָאוּמָּן שֶׁעֲשָׂאַנִי שֶׁלֹּא נָתַן בִּי כֹּחַ יוֹתֵר". שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר הָאָדָם מְצַמְצֵם עַצְמוֹ כְּפִי כֹּחוֹ בְּגוֹדֶל הָעֲבוֹדָה עַד מָקוֹם שֶׁיָּדוֹ מַגַּעַת, וְעַל זֶה הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁאֵין כֹּחַ הָאָדָם מַגִּיעַ וְשׁוֹלֵט שָׁם, כְּמוֹ בְּהוֹלָדָה שֶׁמּוּכְרַחַת לִהְיוֹת עַל יְדֵי שִׁכְחָה וְהֶעְלֵם, אָז יָכוֹל הָאָדָם לְהִשָּׁעֵן עַל הַטַּעֲנָה "לֵךְ לָאוּמָּן שֶׁעֲשָׂאַנִי", הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִגְמוֹר בַּעֲדוֹ לְטוֹב. וּמִמֵּילָא הָאָדָם הַזֶּה יִרְאֶה שֶׁאֵין דָּבָר בָּעוֹלָם מִבַּלְעֲדֵי אֱלֹהִים, אַךְ לְכָל חֵפֶץ יֵשׁ לוֹ הִתְחַבְּרוּת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא בָּרָא כֹּל וּמַנְהִיג אֶת כֹּל וּמוֹשֵׁל בַּכֹּל, וְהָאָדָם מִצִּדּוֹ אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning is this: in this domain there is an extremely great expansion, forgetfulness, and concealment, to the extent that even a righteous person sometimes fathers a wicked person. The beneficial counsel for a person even here is to diminish and restrain this domain according to his capacity. He can then say, “Go to the Craftsman who made me,” who did not give me greater power. When a person restrains himself according to his capacity, through great labor in service, as far as his reach extends, then in the domain where human power does not reach or rule—as in procreation, which necessarily involves forgetfulness and concealment—he can rely on the plea “Go to the Craftsman who made me.” That is, the blessed God will complete the matter for his good. Consequently this person will see that nothing in the world exists apart from God: every thing has a connection to the blessed God, who created everything, governs everything, and rules everything. The person, on his own side, has no independent power at all.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov gives the order of reliance on divine completion in the domain of the covenant. The appeal to the Craftsman follows restraint as far as human power reaches; it is not a substitute for that effort. This explains the precise “after he has refined himself according to his capacity” in Lech Lecha, including why a gift can address what ordinary voluntary control cannot fully secure.

records.originEnglish: Its relation to circumcision follows the verses: “The Lord did not give you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear,” and “I led you,” and “You did not eat bread or drink wine and strong drink.” Once He gave them a heart to know, they merited eyes to see: to see only the blessed God and to learn from all creatures for His service. This resembles the saying in Eruvin: “‘Who teaches us from the beasts of the earth’—had Torah not been given, we would have learned modesty,” and so forth. Likewise in Berakhot: one who sees bread and says, “How beautiful is this bread; blessed is the Omnipresent who created it.” They also merited “ears to hear”: from everything they heard, they would learn for the service of the blessed God, as in “Your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying: This is the way; walk in it,” as we have explained.
records.themeTitle: Perception becomes instruction for chosen service
records.themeSummary: A heart that knows gives direction to seeing and hearing. The ois uses learning from animals and blessing over bread to show how an encounter with Creation can become instruction for service.

records.targetEnglish: A person must learn from them, as they said in Pesachim that Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah learned an a fortiori argument from the frogs. Although the frogs do not possess choice, one nevertheless learns that carrying out the blessed God’s will can include giving up one’s life and the annulment of that thing itself: we saw that God established the frogs of Egypt to perform their action with self-sacrifice when it involved sanctifying His name. All creatures naturally flee what harms them, and from this too we learn, in our chosen conduct, to preserve the body and refrain from its activity even in the commandments of God, corresponding to their natural activity. But in an action involving sanctification of the Name, self-sacrifice is required, as with them. This is “Who teaches us from the beasts of the earth”: in our actions of choice, we learn from them.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains how creatures without free choice can nevertheless teach a person who acts through choice. The observation must be understood in relation to the kind of divine service involved; the passage preserves both bodily self-preservation and the distinct case of sanctification of the Name. This gives method and limits to Lech Lecha’s learning from all creatures, rather than treating every natural behavior as an undifferentiated model to imitate.

records.targetEnglish: After the holy Shabbat of Yitro: what they said in Yoma, that the manna changes into all flavors, refers to the substance of the manna Israel ate. But when the Sages said that goats and deer ate it and the nations tasted manna through their meat, they perceived only manna’s own flavor specified in the Torah, “Like a wafer with honey,” and nothing more. The flavor absorbed in their flesh no longer changed; therefore the nations too could taste it.
records.explanation: In this recorded dream, Rav Tzadok distinguishes the manna’s power to change into many tastes from one taste subsequently absorbed into another food. This gives precision to Lech Lecha’s description of manna as the root of all eating: the multiplicity belongs to the heavenly nourishment itself, rather than every later trace of its flavor. The record is attributed as a dream interpretation, with the quoted distinction preserved.

records.targetEnglish: Matzah is called bread from the earth, in which there is still waste. Eating manna is called bread from Heaven because that bread contained no waste and they did not need to relieve themselves. The bread the companions eat, called “Wisdom gives life to its possessor,” sweetens all the waste and illuminates all the distant places, so that no place is devoid of His light. This is “At first they entered the bread called matzah; now they merited to enter another, higher bread.” By surrendering all their power of action to the blessed God—for chametz indicates human action and matzah the relinquishing of human action—they merited bread from Heaven, entirely clarified of waste. Heaven indicates immense clarity, where it is clear that the blessed God creates and governs; therefore there is no waste at all in this eating.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains what “from Heaven” contributes to the nourishment: clarity about the One who creates and governs removes what cannot be integrated into it. It also distinguishes manna from a further nourishment of wisdom that sweetens even the waste. This illuminates the link between manna, Torah, and perception in Lech Lecha without making all three stages identical.

This follows the saying in Sotah: according to the one who interprets “houses of royalty,” David too descended from Miriam. David is a vehicle for kingship, “the mouth,” the Oral Torah.

records.targetEnglish: The well came in Miriam’s merit, the feminine aspect, as in “A woman who fears the Lord,” for awe is called feminine. King David too descended from Miriam, as our Sages said, “Kings from Miriam,” and this corresponds to the designation of king. The patriarchs’ digging of wells is like “I labored and found.” I heard that after the labor a person finds a found object—something that did not come through his labor, since a find comes unexpectedly, not through labor. Nevertheless, without that labor he would not have found it. Likewise, the water of Miriam’s well was already there, but through the labor of digging one finds it. Thus all a person’s labor is to find that spring flowing within the heart from the source of life, blessed be His name.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim explains the same Miriam–well–David relation through “I labored and found.” Human effort opens access to a spring that it does not itself manufacture, and that spring is located within the heart. This gives depth to the well’s association with Oral Torah in Lech Lecha, alongside Moses’ heavenly bread: discovery involves labor while the life discovered still comes from its divine source.

records.originEnglish: Once they merited a heart to know after forty years—as they derived from this verse in Avodah Zarah, a person does not grasp his teacher’s understanding until forty years—then they likewise merited being given eyes to see and ears to hear, as stated. The same applies to Abraham our father, of whom it is written, “You found his heart faithful before You and made the covenant with him.” When he merited a heart to know, he merited God’s giving him rule over the five organs so that they too would be under his control. Thus, “You set his name as Abraham”: he then merited control over them, hearing and seeing only a matter of mitzvah from which to learn the service of the blessed God, as explained.

records.targetEnglish: The Raaya Meheimna says: “‘You shall know that I am the Lord your God’—this is the first commandment of all the commandments: to know the Holy One, blessed be He, in a general way, that there is a supreme ruler, the Master of the world, who created all the worlds. At the end of forty years of labor, He then taught them in a particular way. This is ‘Know today’: specifically today, when previously they had no permission. ‘That the Lord is God’—this is in a particular way, and many mysteries and secrets are contained in it. This and the first are all one matter: one in general and one in particular.” These are its words. This makes clear what I wrote: the commandment “Know” concerns particular knowledge, by way of the mystery and the secrets of Torah. The precision we noted in “today”—that it is not a command universally applicable like the generality of commandments—is likewise explicit here. They interpret it literally: “today,” after forty years of labor in Torah and commandments. These are the words of the Rambam that one should not enter the orchard until one has filled one’s belly with meat and wine from the revealed aspects of Torah and the commandments.
records.explanation: Sefer HaZikhronot explains the forty years through a progression from general recognition to particular understanding, following sustained Torah and mitzvah practice. This gives content to the ripening of the heart in Lech Lecha. Its distinction between a universal initial obligation and later insight fitted to the learner also prevents “forty years” from becoming a bare calendar formula detached from preparation.

records.targetHebrew: וזה, ולא נתן ד' לכם לב לדעת, שאחר שעברו עליהם במדבר כמה הסתרות, כדכתיב (דברים ח׳:ט״ו) המוליכך במדבר הגדול והנורא נחש שרף ועקב וגו' זה מורה על הסתרות שהיה להם, והם לא רצו להיות בהסתרה, רק הבקיעו כל ההסתרות וממילא ביררו עצמם שאינם חפצים רק ברצון השי"ת, אז אומר השי"ת בן ארבעים לבינה, ונקראים דור דעה, ואין לך דור חביב כדור המדבר. היינו שהעיד עליהם השי"ת שאפילו בתוך ההסתר היו נקשרים בהשי"ת ולא עברו על רצונו ית' אפילו כחוט השערה, וזה ולא נתן ד' לכם לב לדעת וגו' עד היום הזה. וכמו שכתיב בהסדרה הזאת את ד' האמרת היום להיות לך לאלהים וגו' וד' האמירך היום להיות לו לעם סגולה וגו'. וביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה, שהאמרת, הוא מלשון אמרת הבגד. וכמו שבגד כל זמן שאין לה אימרא עדיין לא נגמר הבגד, ועדיין יכול להוסיף עליו ולגרוע ממנו, וכשנגמר האימרא אז הוא הגמר והתכלית הבגד. כך, את ד' האמרת היום להיות לך לאלהים, כי מאחר שביררו ישראל את עצמן לאחר ארבעים שנה שכל תכליתם הוא הכל להיות לך לאלהים, היינו שכל תכלית של ישראל הוא כבוד שמים. וזה וד' האמירך היום להיות לו לעם סגולה, היינו שמראה השי"ת שכל תכליתו הכל בשביל ישראל, וכל בריאת העולם היה הכל בשביל ישראל כדאיתא בתקוני זוה"ק (תיקון סט) ובמדרש (רבה בראשית א) ישראל עלה במחשבה תחלה:
records.targetEnglish: This is “The Lord did not give you a heart to know”: after they had passed through many concealments in the wilderness, as it is written, “Who led you through the great and fearsome wilderness, with fiery serpents and scorpions,” indicating the concealments they experienced, they did not wish to remain in concealment. They broke through all the concealments and thereby clarified themselves as desiring only the will of the blessed God. God then says, “At forty, understanding.” They are called the generation of knowledge, and no generation is as beloved as the wilderness generation. The blessed God testified that even within concealment they were bound to Him and did not depart from His will by even a hair’s breadth. This is “The Lord did not give you a heart to know ... until this day.” Likewise, this portion says, “You have affirmed the Lord today to be your God,” and “The Lord has affirmed you today to be His treasured people.” My revered grandfather explained that he’emarta is related to the hem of a garment. As long as a garment has no hem, it is unfinished, and one can still add to or remove from it; when the hem is completed, the garment reaches its completion. Thus, after Israel clarified itself over forty years so that its entire purpose was “to be your God”—the honor of Heaven—God showed that His entire purpose was for Israel, and all Creation was for Israel, as the Tikkunei Zohar and the Midrash say: Israel arose in thought first.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef interprets the same verse and forty-year teaching through the clarification of what the people truly seek. Passing through concealment establishes that the inward purpose, rather than its outward garment, is desired; the finished hem then represents a settled attainment. This explains why Lech Lecha locates the change in the heart before describing the transformed sight and hearing.

records.targetEnglish: Therefore converts too require immersion before receiving Torah. Although their mazal stood at Mount Sinai, and through this their defilement also ceased, as stated in Shabbat, it nevertheless did not cease immediately at their birth. While still gentiles, they remained like other idolaters who are defiled. Only upon conversion does it cease through their reception of Torah, as for all Israel at the giving of Torah. They therefore need prior immersion in order, through it, to become like a newborn child after receiving Torah: the immersion comes together with their reception of words of Torah. Once Israel was chosen at the giving of Torah, purifying immersion has no application to idolaters at all, for it purifies only by virtue of the Torah’s commandment, and Torah was given only to Israel. In the convert’s case, however, both come together, [as in the principle that her divorce document and her courtyard take effect together].
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim gives an analogous distinction between an outward bodily act and its efficacy as a commanded entry into a new condition. Immersion and reception of Torah take effect together for the convert; the physical action alone does not supply that meaning. This illuminates why Lech Lecha refuses to equate Abraham’s hypothetical earlier cutting with the commanded covenant that makes him a new being.

records.targetEnglish: “God said to Abraham: You shall keep My covenant, you and your descendants after you throughout their generations.” Why did Abraham not fulfill circumcision before he was commanded, when the Talmud says that he fulfilled even eruv tavshilin? All the commandments safeguard a person so that he walks in accordance with “God made the human being upright,” without turning to one side, but following the middle way. If he becomes absorbed in one thing, he alters the straight way and departs from it; Abraham therefore fulfilled all the commandments before being commanded. Circumcision, however, means that the person repairs God’s creation, which was created with a lack. Before he was commanded, he could not on his own change and repair God’s creation, for this would resemble saying, God forbid, “How ugly is this vessel You made.” God therefore showed him Ishmael’s birth. In that birth too he fulfilled God’s will, for Abraham had no merely optional act: all his actions followed God’s will. Afterward he saw that Ishmael’s deeds were not good. From this he understood that God deliberately established a lack for a person to repair, so that it would be credited to the person. He thereby understood that there was room for the commandment of circumcision. He did not see this until Ishmael was grown, thirteen years old. As soon as he understood that there was room for circumcision, God illuminated him and immediately gave him the commandment through an explicit utterance. Such is His will: that human action become manifest and that the person eat from the labor of his hands.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach addresses exactly the same question and explains why circumcision differs from preserving an already upright course. It repairs a lack deliberately left for human work, a purpose Abraham had to recognize and receive by an explicit command. This develops Lech Lecha’s distinction between an earlier physical act and the commanded new creation, while preserving the different role assigned to Ishmael’s birth in Mei HaShiloach’s account.

records.targetEnglish: In truth, the Exodus clarifies this matter: the holiness of each Israelite soul individually, rather than only the general holiness derived from the patriarchs. “Let his men be numbered”: in the count of six hundred thousand, each is considered and counted on his own. I heard that this is the meaning of the census of Israel and the numbering of its people: each is a counted thing, important in himself, and is not nullified within the collective, for he has a particular power not found in everyone. They merited this individual holiness at the giving of Torah and through the Egyptian exile that preceded it. Concerning “a nation from within a nation,” our Sages said: like a fetus within its mother. Ezekiel explicitly calls the redemption from Egypt a birth: “As for your birth, on the day you were born,” and so forth. The Ari likewise explains in Pri Etz Chaim that Egypt was the mystery of gestation; examine it there at length.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim distinguishes the holiness inherited within the patriarchal collective from each descendant’s particular holy contribution, using gestation and birth to describe the transition. This explains what still awaits clarification after the inclusive promise in Lech Lecha. The target’s later discussion gives its own account of sin and judgment in exile; the connection here concerns inherited and individual holiness, not an assertion that the two works give identical explanations of punishment.

records.targetEnglish: At the beginning of the redemption from Egypt, Israel’s clarification began: they did not want any good received through concealed light and disturbed understanding. We see this from their beginning to cry to God: “They cried out, and their cry rose to God.” Although it seemed they lacked nothing, their hearts found no rest in all their good things because these came through concealment of the light. They had begun to recognize this distinction between Israel and the nations, until at redemption they were freed from it completely. Thus we say: “He brought His people Israel out from among them to everlasting freedom.” Although in truth we do not recognize that freedom, since we are still servants, my revered grandfather explained that the principal redemption was the liberation of Israel’s understanding from Egypt. An exile like the one then, in which Israel’s understanding was occupied and distracted, will not recur. Even amid every distraction, an Israelite’s heart cries to God to see His light. This clarification was completed in the wilderness, for of that generation it is written, “Your following after Me in the wilderness.” The wilderness indicates concealed light, as in “Who led you through the wilderness, fiery serpents and scorpions.” These indicate the concealments they experienced; nevertheless, Scripture testified, “Your following after Me.” Though God hid the light of His face from them, their principal desire was to recognize His light, and they did not want concealment. This is “the love of your bridal days”: Israel’s principal longing and love is to be included in His light. Through this they became completely clarified, as the verse concludes, “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first of His produce.”
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef identifies an inward clarification within the movement out of Egypt: the heart ceases to be satisfied with good received in concealment and seeks the divine source of that good. Its account of continuing desire in later exile explains why “everlasting freedom” is not equated with constant outward freedom. This supplies a concrete form of the people’s clarification described at the end of Lech Lecha, including its continuation through the wilderness. Editorial citation note: “Who led you through the wilderness…” is Deuteronomy 8:15; the inherited Hebrew locator דברים ה is preserved.
